#4523. The Most Expensive Ford Fathom Electric Truck Will Still Start Under $40,000: Report

The Ford Fathom will arrive for the 2028 model year in multiple trim levels, according to the Detroit Free Press, but they’ll all be reasonably priced.

Ford’s new affordable mid-size electric truck was announced earlier this year, and company executives are now hinting at how much even the nicest Fathom pickup will cost, according to The Detroit Free Press.

We already know a base model Ford Fathom will start at $29,945, including a $1595 destination charge. But Andrew Frick, president of Ford’s Model e division, told the Detroit Free Press that even a fully-loaded Fathom won’t crest $40,000. That’s some serious value for a truck that is set to offer a touchscreen, built-in Apple Maps, Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, and Blue Cruise hands-free driving capabilities.

"We'll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range.  And we'll have a couple different offerings within that," said to the Detroit Free Press. "If you know that nearly fifty percent of the U.S. new vehicle industry transacts under $40,000, not only do we expect Fathom ... to attract new and used EV buyers, but also (gasoline) and hybrid customers, especially because we're going to have much lower operating costs than even a mainstream hybrid vehicle."

Ford CEO Jim Farley was duly impressed during a test drive of the Fathom. "It completely blew me away. Zero to sixty is huge … and the hands-free experience was like something I've never experienced. Fathom is really a breakthrough product. It's highly capable, innovative, affordable,” Farley said during a Wall Street analyst meeting on October 28.

Designers at Ford told Road & Track earlier this year that the Fathom will be spacious, too, as the four-door pickup will have more passenger volume than a Toyota RAV4. Additionally, the truck is being used to pilot a new “Universal EV Production System” at its Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky. With over $2 billion invested in retooling the plant, Ford is betting big on the new production process and its 400-volt Universal EV platform, which will launch with the Fathom.

Details about the Fathom’s powertrain and specific trim levels have yet to be announced. The all-electric pickup truck is set to arrive in late 2027, but pre-orders will open in the first quarter of that year.

#4522. These Are the Bestselling Electric Pickup Trucks

A total of 232,809 electric pickup trucks have sold since the start of 2024. Ford alone sells nearly that many gas-powered F-series pickups every single quarter.

Electric pickup trucks are still a relatively new idea, but they've now been along long enough to gather some data on how they're selling. We totaled sales numbers from 2024, 2025, and 2026 so far to see which electric pickup trucks have had the biggest impact on the market in the past few years.

For some perspective, electric pickups still make up a tiny portion of the overall truck market in the U.S. Even if you combine the sales of all six models listed here, over a time period of nearly three years, you get 232,809 units sold in total. Ford sold 801,525 units of the F-series pickup in 2025 alone. There are also aren’t any pickup trucks on our list of the bestselling EVs in 2026, a list which contains mostly SUVs.

The sales totals for each model listed here include figures from the full-year 2024, the full-year 2025, and through the third quarter of 2026. In cases where the automaker doesn't release detailed sales figures, we used estimates from Cox Automotive.

If you feel like you see Cybertrucks everywhere you go, that's not just because their distinctive styling makes them stand out on the road. Tesla has sold quite a few pickup trucks in the past few years, which may seem surprising given the Cybertruck's polarizing design and numerous recalls early in its production run. Tesla started selling the Cybertruck in 2024, and that was the strongest year of sales, suggesting that eager early adopters made up much of the early run of 38,965 units sold that year. Sales declined to around 20,000 units in 2025, and through the third quarter of 2026 Tesla has moved an estimated 11,586 units.

Ford was one of the first to enter the electric-truck market, and its strategy hinged on the F-150 Lightning's similarities to the top-selling F-150 pickup. The F-150 Lightning has since been discontinued, ending production in 2025, but it managed to rack up a significant number of sales. Keep in mind that the Lightning went on sale for the 2022 model year, well before many of the other models on this list, so the sales totals here reflect only the latter half of its production run.

General Motors' Hummer EV pickup was also early to the trend, debuting for the 2022 model year like the F-150 Lightning. But it took a completely different approach with its wild styling, mega-horsepower powertrain, and ridiculous off-road capability. GMC added an SUV sibling for 2024, and the caveat to the Hummer's sales numbers are that they include both body styles. We aren't able to break out numbers for just the pickup, because GM doesn't report those figures separately.

Chevy's electric version of the Silverado pickup got off to a slow start, racking up less than 8000 sales in 2024, its first year on the market. Those numbers picked up for 2025 as Chevrolet added lower-cost variants meant for fleets, cresting 11,000 units that year. But it appears demand has softened once again, as Chevy only moved 5327 units through the first three quarters of this year.

Rivian's debut model was the R1T, which was exactly as innovative as you would expect from a startup automaker. With impressive performance, futuristic styling, and new ideas such as a storage tunnel between the cab and the bed, the R1T aimed more at lifestyle buyers than at traditional pickup customers. The R1T went on sale for the 2022 model year, and sales have been on a steady decline since 2024, Rivian's recently launched compact R2 SUV is now outselling the larger R1 lineup, which makes us wonder if there is room for Rivian to add a pickup version of that model that would offer a lower cost of entry.

Riding on the same platform as the Chevrolet Silverado EV, the Sierra EV aims for a middle ground between GM's other electric pickups. It's more upscale than its Chevy sibling, especially in Denali trim, but far more conventional-looking than the other GMC EV truck, the wild Hummer EV. Its sales numbers followed a similar trend as the Chevy, with a slow start in 2024, a rise in 2025, and a drop again in 2026.

#4521. This Slammed ’55 Chevy Bel Air Restomod Packs a 741-HP V-8

Built by CAL Automotive Creations and featuring a giant V-8, this ‘55 Chevy was among the many custom builds shown at SEMA.

People have been modifying classic cars for ages, and the Chevy Bel Air is a perfect candidate. CAL Automotive Creations got its hands on a 1955 two-door model and decided it needed a massive V-8, which BluePrint Engines was happy to provide.

Paired with a Bowler automatic gearbox, the crate engine is covered in deep red paint and outfitted with an EFI intake, machined valve covers, and fabricated stainless-steel headers. The 598-cubic-inch V-8, which produces 741 horsepower and 703 pound-feet of torque, breathes through SpinTech mufflers.

Additionally, CAL thoroughly reworked the Art Morrison chassis, creating rear rails that turn upward for a lower ride height in combination with RideTech coil-overs. Raising the center crossmembers ensure that components remain above the scrub line, meaning it’s drivable even on pockmarked roads.

Of course, the exterior received attention as well. Reshaped quarter panels, taillight bezels, and a front grille surround are examples of where CAL demonstrated its craftsmanship. The dark paint and bodywork were specially made for this build, accompanied by nickel touches from Advanced Plating. Leading Edge Machine and Design is responsible for the one-off wheels, which match the paint. A staggered setup gives the Bel Air an even more aggressive look.

The interior was a product of CAL and Santana Interior Design, and though the cabin still has a classic look with its billet-machined center console (featuring cupholders under the slidable armrest), it is equipped with Dakota digital instrumentation and Vintage Air climate control.

#4520. Range Rover is axing its two cheapest SUVs, making way for a new entry-level EV

Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in.

For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.

That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.

In the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.

Range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.

While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.

Range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.

The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range said, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.

It’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s new EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover plans to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.

Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).

The Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).

Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.

At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.

#4519. Nearly 1 In 3 Hyundais Sold In October Was A Hybrid As High Gas Prices Push Buyers To Pivot

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

A whopping 29% of Hyundai’s total October sales volume in the U.S. were hybrids, the automaker said Tuesday. That’s the highest mix ever for gas-electric powertrains for the Korean automaker, thanks to buyers seeking more fuel efficient cars due to gas prices that have remained stubbornly high since the start of the U.S. war in Iran.

Hyundai doesn't break out hybrid sales in its monthly reports, instead bundling them together under individual model names. But it did say that hybrid versions of the Santa Fe and Palisade set new October sales records. Meanwhile, sales of the all-electric Ioniq 5 bounced back, climbing 21% year over year to 1,981 units.

Hyundai sold 73,452 vehicles in October, a 5% increase over the same month last year. Its year-to-date sales now stand at 770,916 units, up 3% from 2025.

Sister brand Kia also reported record overall and electrified vehicle sales. It sold 80,008 vehicles last month, bringing its year-to-date total to 747,394 units, not far behind Hyundai.

Kia's hybrid sales jumped 114% year over year, helped by strong demand for hybrid versions of the popular Sportage and Sorento SUVs and the Carnival minivan. But the more interesting news is the recovery in Kia's EV sales, which have struggled for several quarters.

Sales of the three-row EV9 surged 111% to 1,406 units, while EV6 sales climbed 58% to 803 units. Kia also sold 976 units of the more affordable EV3, whose production and deliveries are still ramping up following its recent U.S. launch.

There's a caveat to those EV growth figures, though. The Ioniq 5, EV6, and EV9 were all coming off a particularly weak October 2025, when sales cratered following the expiration of the federal EV tax credit a month earlier.

The months leading up to the September 2025 deadline saw buyers rush to claim the incentive, pulling demand forward and causing subsequent sales to decline. The broader EV market has been gradually recovering since, with the third quarter marking its strongest performance since then.

The EV3, meanwhile, could give Kia's electric lineup another shot in the arm. Starting at $31,385 including destination, it's among the cheapest EVs on sale in the U.S., alongside the Nissan Leaf and Chevrolet Bolt. We recently reviewed the small electric crossover and think it offers really good value.

Hyundai could also see another boost to its EV business in the coming months. The automaker is preparing to supply Waymo with tens of thousands of Ioniq 5-based robotaxis, Hyundai CEO José Muñoz said in September. That could be a new source of demand for its electric crossover, beyond individual consumers.

#4516. 10 Action-Adventure Games That Are Unexpected Masterpieces

Ronald is a video game journalist with more than 10 years of experience in the industry, working on several of the most important Spanish websites.

The action-adventure genre is one of the broadest in the entire video game industry, encompassing countless experiences ranging from stealth and hack-and-slash to horror and beat 'em ups.

Thanks to this broad definition, countless masterpieces fall under its umbrella, including many that, unfortunately, haven't achieved the popularity they deserve due to fierce competition.

Even within the realm of major blockbusters, not all underrated titles are obscure indie games—there are games that have fallen just short of mainstream success, though I'm here to help rectify that.

So, in order to shed light on some lesser-known campaigns that haven't yet cemented their undeniable excellence in the collective consciousness, I invite you to explore this list of ten action-adventure games that are unexpected masterpieces.

As the least recognized work from Tango Gameworks, a studio that has certainly gifted us with numerous magnificent journeys, Ghostwire: Tokyo stands out among the games with the greatest disparity between its quality and its fame.

Boasting one of the finest atmospheres crafted this decade, wandering the streets of Shibuya, soaring across rooftops, and taking down the most terrifying yokai imaginable is, by far, one of my highlights of the decade.

Whether in stealth or direct magical combat, tackling one of its turbulent side quests or hunting for collectibles, the game strikes an outstanding balance between making each mechanic satisfying while still maintaining a constant sense of terror in its setting.

As far as first-person games go, Ghostwire: Tokyo is part of the most immersive, rewarding, and distinctive I've played this generation, which is saying something considering the titans with which it shares category.

As the years have gone by, games that adhere to the Metroidvania philosophy have become one of my greatest obsessions, which inevitably led me to fall in love with Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo.

Its ability to capture the nostalgia of the Game Boy Advance era while boasting the refined design and execution of modern products demonstrates its creators' immeasurable talent, who also imbued it with an impressive thematic personality.

The critiques of various strategic production industries resonate with our current times, while in the process, the game leverages the yoyo as a central gameplay element to make traversal, combat, exploration, and customization an absolute delight that's also pretty unique.

Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo is among the finest indie titles I've enjoyed in the last couple of years, and anything other than recognizing it as brilliant is to underestimate its potential.

If you're interested in unfairly criticized titles, I recommend checking out these ten underrated action-adventure games that were badly reviewed.

As someone who didn't experience the franchise's heyday, Shinobi: Art of Vengeance not only caught me completely off guard, but I can think of very few resurrections that have felt so powerful.

The absolute masterwork of action and platforming that this title is results in frankly mind-blowing sequences, flowing seamlessly between both dimensions to deliver a thrilling adventure that doesn't let you breathe for a second.

As you unlock combos, powers, and movement abilities, you encounter an ever-increasing series of challenges that push the game's mechanics to their limits, which are meticulously refined to ensure you have complete control over every pixel.

Few titles in 2025 felt as satisfying to complete 100%, so Shinobi: Art of Vengeance stands as a masterfully unexpected example that, when you don't know what to do with your old IPs, outsourcing to an indie studio to work on them is the best possible idea.

The Legend of Zelda's heirs number in the hundreds of thousands, but that didn't stop Death's Door from emerging as one of its most intelligent and charismatic great-great-grandchildren.

The game perfectly understands the enjoyment that lies in discovery and exploration through iteration, inviting us on a diverse adventure with plenty of colorful biomes, enemies, characters, and circumstances that evoke all kinds of emotions.

Curiosity, fear, happiness, sadness, worry... The title silently manages a multitude of emotions both thematically and in its gameplay, limiting progression to allow for exploration of its expansive world at a prodigious pace.

When discussing isometric titles that combine action, platforming, and puzzles in the best possible way, Death's Door is at the description's forefront, though it's the ease and finesse with which it achieves this that's truly unexpected.

Castlevania is a series that went through some difficult years after the turn of the century, and it wasn't until Castlevania: Lords of Shadow arrived that the IP unexpectedly found some relief amidst so many setbacks, astonishingly becoming the best-selling game in the entire IP.

MercurySteam crafted one of the most beautiful and satisfying hack-and-slash games in the genre's history, finally adapting the saga's formula perfectly to 3D without losing an ounce of its core identity.

The whip feels better than ever, as do the movement mechanics, the puzzles, and the progression systems, all enhanced in the best possible way thanks to a magnificently crafted story and characters that keep you on the edge of your seat until the very last second.

Castlevania: Lords of Shadow completely forgoes being conceptually innovative, but the sacrifice, given it guaranteed us an extremely excellent title in all its facets, was totally worth it even when nobody was betting on such a resounding success.

If you enjoy discovering incredible titles without proper recognition, I recommend these ten best action-adventure games forgotten by time.

In the years when God of War slowed down, and Devil May Cry practically disappeared, a third icon emerged from absolutely nowhere to keep the hack-and-slash genre alive (with Bayonetta's permission): Darksiders.

Drawing inspiration from both Santa Monica Studio's work and The Legend of Zelda, Vigil Games crafted a splendidly elaborate tale and setting within Judeo-Christian mythology, one of the least explored in the video game industry.

Giant bosses based on satisfying gimmicks, varied and refreshing puzzles that make the most of War's arsenal and movement capabilities, phenomenal art design for both environments and enemies... It's the complete package.

That the company's first title would be such a presentation of knowledge in the genre's fundamentals was unforeseen even for the team itself, but much more for the hundreds of thousands who, like me, stumbled upon Darksiders by chance and have been hooked ever since.

Returning to the topic of franchises forced to reinvent themselves to adapt to modern times, not even the most optimistic projections for the Tomb Raider reboot could have predicted the absolute brilliance it would become.

Going back to Lara Croft's origins resulted in one of the quintessential action-adventure games of the entire generation, achieving an astonishing symphony of survival mechanics, realistic yet compelling gunplay, and simply fantastic settings and stories.

Each set piece surpasses the last, and the spectacular scenery contrasts perfectly with the brutal and tense story the legendary archaeologist faces, all while possessing the intriguing premise of not yet being the intrepid adventurer we all know, but rather a young, still-innocent graduate.

From concept to execution, Tomb Raider is a tapestry of sound decisions that, among other things, reminded Uncharted fans that Nathan Drake only managed to run because Lara Croft walked first.

I know that nowadays we're used to indie masterpieces being released every couple of months, but back in the day, before that was the norm, Hyper Light Drifter arrived like a hurricane of grandeur.

Taking Dark Souls' harshness, non-linearity, and disorientation, Heart Machine assembled an adventure that is both cryptic and captivating, where the gameplay and narrative direction are entirely in the player's hands.

Where to go and why are questions that only the user can answer through exploration, embarking on an intense and introspective journey where bosses and secrets abound, motivating us to explore every last corner of its silent world.

Along with gorgeous pixel art, a remarkable sound design, and a simple yet perfect gameplay loop, Hyper Light Drifter built a castle with just a few blocks, a feat reserved only for the greatest.

If you're looking for modern games to get lost in, I recommend the ten best adventure games of the 2020s (so far).

The reviews for Asura's Wrath were so scathing that it took me a decade to finally deign to play it, and the sheer shock of finishing it in tears when the credits rolled was beyond words.

Yes, every single one of the comments regarding its poor gameplay was, is, and will be correct, since it's a beat 'em up where the best parts of the gameplay are the on-rails shooting and quick-time events, and that doesn't exactly reflect well on a title of this genre.

Regardless, when you have such an incredible plot, abundant with charismatic characters, memorable scenes, robust mythology, and eccentrically immeasurable cinematics, I couldn't care less that every encounter boils down to mashing the attack button a hundred times a second.

The intercosmic scale that Asura's Wrath handles in its presentation and spectacle is monumental, unique, and emotional enough to overlook its mediocre mechanics, being the only case in the entire genre where it's a masterpiece even without being fun in the traditional sense.

Bucking the trend in the genre, whose disdain for stealth became evident in the last decade, Arkane Studios made a tremendous statement in 2012 with Dishonored's release.

Coming from another underrated gem, Dark Messiah of Might and Magic, the studio embraced the lingering force of immersive sims and materialized it into a project that excels as both a stealth game and an action-adventure game.

Boasting some of the best level design in video game history, along with a story that evolves based on the player's actions rather than dialogue choices, Dishonored is one of the century's defining power fantasies.

Between Dunwall's perfect setting, the outstanding array of gadgets and powers that allow for creative and expansive use of stealth and violence, and the majestic musical pieces that accompany us, it's clear that the love for stealth games will never die as long as this IP remains available.

Years go by, and I still wonder if the genre has enough strength to produce a title that surpasses Dishonored, but for now, it remains on the throne without any concern about being replaced.

In this list, we'll discuss our picks for the best action-adventure games that go beyond a hundred hours, from RPGs to known open-world titles.

#4515. Defying Online Backlash, The Ferrari Luce EV Is Already Sold Out Through 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Ferrari's first all-electric model is already sold out for 2027, the automaker said during its third-quarter earnings call Tuesday. The Luce starts at an eye-watering $560,800 in the U.S., but neither its price nor its controversial design appears to be putting off Ferrari's deep-pocketed clientele.

“The Luce that we plan to sell next year basically are all allocated,” Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna said in the earnings call. He added that customers placing an order now would have to wait a year to take delivery. Ferrari didn't disclose how many units it plans to sell or provide a regional breakdown of its orders.

Designed through a collaboration with former Apple design chief Jony Ive's LoveFrom, the first electric Prancing Horse looks nothing like the Ferraris we're used to seeing. It trades the brand's signature aggressive, low-slung proportions for a higher-riding silhouette with an industrial-design aesthetic. The Luce is also Ferrari's first-ever five-seat car. The radical departure hasn't gone down particularly well with critics, many of whom have questioned whether the design looks like a Ferrari at all.

Ferrari isn't alone in taking a more unconventional approach to EV design. Jaguar's new Type 01 and the all-electric Mercedes-AMG GT have also sparked plenty of debate. Key rival Lamborghini, meanwhile, has scrapped plans for its first-ever EV, opting to stick with hybrids and gas models for now.

Vigna, however, said buyers were better understanding the Luce after seeing it in person and getting behind the wheel. “We see when and how the perception changes when the people drive the car,” he said.

Early media reviews appear to support that argument. A handful of outlets have already had the opportunity to drive the Luce, and the initial impressions have been overwhelmingly positive. MotorTrend, for instance, described its driving dynamics as “beguilingly natural in its responses, fluid and concise in its change of direction, and beautifully balanced through all phases of a corner.”

The Luce is a beast on paper. It's equipped with quad motors—one at each wheel—for a total of 1,035 horsepower and 730 pound-feet of torque. That's enough to rocket the Luce to 62 mph in 2.5 seconds, Ferrari says. The EV also has rear-wheel steering and a suspension setup derived from the F80 supercar. Steering wheel-mounted paddles let the driver jack up torque or regenerative braking, which is supposed to make the car more engaging to drive.

The EV-specific specs are less impressive for a half-million-dollar car. The Luce's 112-kilowatt-hour battery uses SK On pouch cells and provides 530 kilometers (329 miles) of range on Europe's WLTP cycle. That should translate to somewhere under 300 miles when it gets an EPA rating. Peak charging power lands at 350 kilowatts, which is plenty strong in objective terms but falls short of some of the fastest-charging EVs. But then again, you don't buy a $560,000 Luce because you're looking for a great, practical electric car.

And if there were any doubts about how much wealthy collectors are willing to pay for Ferrari's first EV, consider what happened in August. The first production Luce, dubbed “Chassis 0,” fetched a staggering $40 million at auction, making it the most expensive new car ever sold at auction.

#4514. Ford Fathom EV pickup prices will range from $28,350 to the high $30Ks

Ford’s upcoming Fathom electric pickup will be among the most affordable EVs in the US, starting at $28,350. Even pricier trims will start at under $40,000.

After announcing the name of its new midsize electric pickup this summer, Ford said the Fathom will start at just $28,350 for the standard-range model.

Even with the $1,595 delivery fee, prices will start at under $30,000. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Jim Farley said the Fathom, Ford’s first vehicle off the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform, remains on track to launch in Q4 2027.

Last Tuesday, a day before earnings, Farley said he had the chance to test-drive a prototype and that it “completely blew me away.”

The 0 to 60 mph, huge room inside, and the hands-free, ADAS experience was like “something I’ve never experienced,” Farley told investors.

Ford’s CEO added that the Fathom is a “breakthrough product” that’s highly capable and affordable. The MSRP under $30,000 and low cost of ownership, Farley said, is perfect for today’s market.

The electric pickup will use a zonal electrical architecture and a 48-volt system to cut costs. It will also offer bidirectional charging, enabling it to power your home to save on energy costs or during an outage.

When asked how the company plans to upsell the Fathom beyond the $28,350 starting price, Andrew Frick, president of Ford Model e, offered some insight.

“The starting price of $28,350 is just that,” Frick said. “We’ll have a range that goes to the high $30,000 range. And we’ll have a couple of different offerings within that,” he explained.

Frick said it’s too soon to share more about the offerings themselves at this point, and more details will come closer to launch.

According to Farley, the embedded Apple Maps is a “game changer” for any EV, but especially for a vehicle starting under $30,000.

“That is going to be the most exciting upsell opportunity,” Farley said, “it’s really the long-term subscription and digital experience for the customer.”

Apple Maps will be directly integrated into the navigation system. All Fathom models will be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving with standard Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

We still haven’t seen the interior, but Ford claims the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with easy-to-use navigation.

I almost feel like the Fathom will be utilized similarly to how the Maverick is utilized and possibly become a big seller as well. It seems well suited for a small business work vehicle as well with fuel savings by going electric to add to the appeal.

The midsize electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, and that’s not including the frunk (front trunk) or truck bed. Ford also said the Fathom will cost less to own over five years than a three-year-old used Tesla Model Y.

We also know the Fathom will have an NACS port after a prototype was caught at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.

Ford is set to open preorders in early 2027, with an official launch expected in the fourth quarter of 2027.

#4512. GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:

According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

#4511. Used EVs Are Selling Like Hotcakes. The Fastest Movers May Surprise You

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Used EVs are getting more popular. Not only are they increasing in popularity, they're selling even faster than their hybrid and even gasoline counterparts, according to iSeeCars.

You might assumed that all of the used Teslas hitting the market would be a big reason why. But in reality, no Tesla even cracked the top 10 list of best-selling used EVs in September 2026.

Compared to the same month last year, this September saw a 9.8% price increase for used EVs. That's exactly double the 4.8% increase used hybrids saw year-over-year. However, both absolutely crush used gas car values, which only jumped 0.3%. You can bet that high fuel prices over the past year or so have had an affect on gas and diesel demand. People are thinking about EVs more than ever before, especially every time the see eye-watering receipts from every fill up.

“These pricing shifts reflect significantly different year-over-year trends across drivetrains,” iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer said in a release. “Ongoing higher fuel prices are likely driving the shift, though the EV segment has also recovered from the demand turbulence caused by the loss of federal incentives a year ago.”

Price isn't the only indicator of demand, though. Speed is another. Used EVs fly off the figurative shelves faster than gas cars, spending an average of 41.9 days on the lot. Not only is that 10.1% faster than September 2025, but it's almost two weeks faster on average than gas cars, which take 54.8 days to sell. Furthermore, gas car sale time increased by 19.9%. So it's getting harder to sell used gas cars, while EVs are getting easier.

Admittedly, in defense of gas cars, customers are spoiled for choice. There are far, far more gas cars available for sale—for example, Autotrader lists 1,384,383 used gas and diesel cars nationwide, but only 44,434 used EVs. There are also fewer EV models for sale, so customers aren't cross-shopping as much. Still, there's no denying that used EV demand is increasing as supply continues to grow.

There are also more options than ever in a market that was once essentially wholly dominated by Tesla. But in September, none of the top 10 fastest-selling used EV models were Teslas. There weren't any Lucids or Rivians in there, either. The quickest-selling EVs were oddly the Audi Q4 E-tron Sportback, followed by the Toyota bZX4, and Lexus RZ 300e. So it seems that used EV customers are becoming like everyone else: they just want something small and practical, with some quirky styling and a nice interior. Also on the list were the Honda Prologue, BMW iX, and even Polestar 2.

The slowest-selling EVs aren't exactly surprising, though, as they're mostly massive and expensive SUVs and trucks. The Cadillac Escalade IQ was the slowest-seller by a huge margin, but it's also uber-expensive. It was followed by the GMC Sierra EV, Chevy Silverado EV, and the Volvo EX90. The Hummer EV was on the list, too, proving that GM's Ultium trucks aren't exactly popular on the used market.

One of the reasons why used Teslas might not have sold as quickly as other EVs is that their prices have increased. The Tesla Model S and Model X both saw used price increases of 22% and 18%, respectively. That is good for the two highest of any used car on the market, regardless of powertrain.

It's interesting to see used EVs increasing in selling speed, showing that customers are willing to go electric when the vehicle type and price suits their needs. And now that data has come out proving that EVs don't lose as much range over time as previously thought, it seems that used EVs are becoming better and better buys.

#4509. First: Volvo CE Electric equipment does the work, without disturbing the wildlife

For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a big impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

#4508. Renault’s Latest EV Was Designed For The Army’s Toughest Missions

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Renault Group has developed an all-electric, all-wheel-drive modular electric vehicle for military operations. Dubbed the Forefront Concept, it uses proven automotive components to keep costs down and boost production times.

The electric field vehicle was designed for both defense and civilian applications, and can be remotely operated by a human or sent into high-risk, hard-to-reach areas on its own, using its autonomous driving capabilities.

Renault Group built the vehicle, while John Cockerill designed the EV’s remote-operation and autonomy functions. The defense company listened to input from the French armed forces, which will use the Forefront Concept in several exercises and trials in the coming weeks to put it through its paces. After the trials, Renault will further refine the concept based on operational feedback.

Powered by two electric motors, the cab-less field machine has four-wheel steering and can travel in complete silence in some of the harshest terrain. The French automaker said the projected range is roughly 250 miles (400 kilometers) on a full charge, but an add-on range extender can further extend the driving distance. That said, Renault didn’t say how much energy the on-board battery or range extender can store.

With a 2,200-pound (1-tonne) payload, the dual-motor buggy can be used for logistics support, anti-drone operations, fire support, and evacuation. In highly disputed areas, sending in a vehicle that doesn’t have a human behind a steering wheel means fewer potential casualties. At the same time, the Forefront Concept can be used by companies that need a safe way to access dangerous sites.

Renault Group said the remotely-operated EV was designed to be quickly put into production at competitive costs. There’s no price yet, but if there’s enough interest, we might see the boxy R/C car for adults become a reality sooner rather than later.

As the world’s battlefields continue to transform into places where machines do the heavy lifting while being controlled from hundreds of miles away by human operators, vehicles like Renault’s Forefront will become increasingly ubiquitous.

Ukrainian companies have churned out thousands of remotely controlled robots in the fight against Russia. The models range from pint-sized mini-tanks to big drones that can airlift wounded soldiers.

Over in the United States, the Army has recently awarded an 18-month contract to American Rheinmetall to develop and deliver the next generation of uncrewed ground vehicles (UGV). The cab-less prototype is based on Harbinger’s extended-range EV platform, which uses a gas engine as a generator for an all-electric powertrain.

With a full tank of gas and a full battery, the military-grade plug-in hybrid can deliver over 500 miles of range, with the big benefit being its ability to shut off the gas engine for silent operations. Compared to Renault’s new concept, the Harbinger-based UGV platform can accommodate larger and heavier payloads of up to 18,000 lbs.

#4506. High gas prices are pumping up used EV sales: these are FLYING off the lot

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

#4505. Mercedes Wants To Rethink EV Batteries With This Clever New Technology

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Mercedes-Benz wants to flip the script on how electric car high-voltage batteries work. Its new Power Converter, which is still in the development stage, can control the charge and discharge of individual cells inside the battery, which is a big change from how the vast majority of EV batteries work today.

For decades, traction batteries have had thousands of individual cells, which are arranged into cell groups or modules. The car’s brain can monitor the voltage of each cell or module, but when it comes to charging or discharging, everything gets the same treatment. Does the electric motor require 100 kilowatts? The whole pack delivers 100 kW. Charging at 150 kW? All the cells get treated equally.

With Mercedes’ new technology, however, each cell inside the pack can not only be monitored, but also controlled by a programmable micro-converter. In theory, the approach has a lot of advantages, including prolonging a car’s battery life, using different cell chemistries inside the same pack, and removing bulky power electronics that handle AC and DC conversion.

Let’s look at the longevity aspect first. When an EV battery fails, it’s usually because one or more cells inside the pack can no longer sustain the same voltage as their neighbors. The car throws a scary error message on the screen, and the dealer or service center will recommend replacing the entire battery, which costs a lot of money if the warranty has run out.

With Mercedes-Benz’s new approach, if a cell can no longer sustain the required voltage, it can be simply disabled by its micro-converter. Sure, the battery capacity goes down a smidge, but the car will still work as before.

By using multiple converters in parallel, the system can regulate the energy flow of individual cells or cell groups, removing the need for a single big converter. What’s more, if cells of varying chemistries or ages are bundled in the same pack, the micro-converters can make sure that they all get charged properly, albeit at different power levels. The same goes for the high-voltage output, which will no longer be tied to the number of cells connected in series, but to the converters and their software-based control.

The technology also enables a more modular approach to battery use. For instance, if a large-capacity battery isn’t used at full potential most of the time—say the owner drives only 50 miles daily—the car’s brain can put part of the pack in standby mode, keeping the cells at the right level for preservation. Then, when a long-distance road trip is being planned, the computer can unlock the full capacity.

Bidirectional charging is baked into the Power Converter. This means that AC and DC conversion, as well as bidirectional charging, are handled directly by the micro-converters, enabling finer control over how the battery is used.

Mercedes-Benz said that the new technology has the potential to boost the driving range and efficiency of future plug-in models, though there is one big asterisk that the company conveniently left out. With thousands of micro-converters sealed inside a battery pack, it inevitably means that there are thousands of components that can fail. If done right, though, it can bring a new level of modularity and fine-tuning to EV batteries.

#4504. BLUETTI’s flexible $1,099 Apex 200 backs up your home – and powers your RV

What do you actually need to keep running when the power goes out? For most households, the fridge, wifi, phones, and a few other essentials come first. Buying enough battery storage for every appliance in the house can come later – and that’s the appeal of BLUETTI’s latest launch, the Apex 200 portable power station.

The Apex 200 starts with 2.56kWh of storage and 3.2kW of continuous AC output, with the option to add batteries when you need longer backup. Built-in RV connections also mean it can earn its keep between blackouts.

BLUETTI launches the Apex 200 on November 4, with standalone super early-bird pricing starting at $1,099 through November 18. Electrek readers can get an extra 5% off with code ELECTREK5OFF.

Here’s how to work out which setup is worth buying for your home or RV.

The Apex 200 takes the expandable design of BLUETTI’s flagship Apex series and puts it in a smaller package.

You get a 2,560Wh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. The 3.2kW of continuous AC output increases to 3.6kW when an expansion battery is connected or the unit is actively charging.

The enclosure holds all that in 36.2 liters and weighs 26.9kg (59.3 lb). You’ll want two hands to move it, but it’s convenient to move it between home and your camper.

BLUETTI’s UltraCell technology delivers an industry-leading energy density of 70.7 Wh/L, yet the Apex 200 is more than 50% smaller by volume than class competitors. For an RV owner, that smaller footprint frees up room for other gear.

There’s also a tilted display and four app-controllable AC outlets. That might not sound like a big deal, but when the battery is on the floor or under your desk and you want to check or redirect its charge, it means you don’t have to crouch.

BLUETTI calls its approach “Start Small. Scale Big. Power More.” BLUETTI says Apex 300 users reported liking the modular design but wanted something easier to handle day to day. The Apex 200 offers them a lower entry point, with room to add capacity rather than replace the main unit.

Before buying a portable power station, you’ll want to know how much power your appliances draw and how much energy they use over time.

For example, a 150W appliance running continuously for 10 hours uses 1,500Wh. A 1,500W appliance gets through that same amount in one hour. Running a coffee maker briefly is a different proposition from keeping a high-draw appliance on all afternoon.

A rough runtime calculation is: Usable battery capacity in watt-hours ÷ average load in watts = hours of operation.

Divide the Apex 200’s nominal 2,560Wh by a steady 150W load, and you get about 17 hours before accounting for conversion losses and the battery system’s own power use. Real runtime will be lower.

Refrigerators complicate that calculation because their compressors cycle on and off. Check measured daily energy use where possible, along with startup demand – motors can briefly draw more power when they kick on.

If your usual blackout lasts four to 12 hours, start by looking at the Apex 200 on its own.

BLUETTI estimates it can run a 150W refrigerator for 10–12 hours, or support low-draw essentials such as CPAPs, wifi routers, and mobile devices for two to three days, depending on the equipment and how it’s used. That doesn’t mean every device on that list will run together for three days. Your combined load determines the runtime.

The Apex 200 also gives you more control over where that energy goes. Four independently controllable Smart AC outlets built right into the unit – no need to buy smart plugs! – let you switch individual devices on and off through the BLUETTI App, set schedules, and apply state-of-charge controls. So if something doesn’t need power overnight, you can turn off its power at the outlet and save the fridge’s battery.

BLUETTI calls the feature an industry first for portable power stations. The system also works with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant.

A UPS function switches connected equipment to battery power in 15 milliseconds. Check that switching time against your equipment’s requirements, especially for a CPAP or other sensitive device.

With AC output on and the display off, idle consumption drops to just 10.5W.

A winter freeze or severe storm can leave you without grid power for days. That’s when adding extra storage starts to make more sense.

For typical power outages, adding one or two BLUETTI B300K batteries can extend essential home backup to two to three days.

But you can go further. One Apex 200 supports up to six B500K expansion batteries, bringing its maximum capacity to 33.28kWh.

But a bigger battery still needs recharging eventually. The Apex 200 accepts up to 3kW of solar input across two independent channels:

With a correctly configured array of SORA 500 portable solar panels making full use of those inputs, BLUETTI says the base battery can charge from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes, or reach 100% in 1.7 hours using solar alone.

A solar generator setup lets you recharge during daylight. The Apex 200 can also be charged with wall AC, vehicle charging, and compatible gas-generator charging. A suitable 30A generator connection can help replenish the battery when solar production falls short.

The Apex 200 can also form part of a larger home battery backup system through BLUETTI’s Hub A1 parallel box.

BLUETTI specifies up to 6kW of continuous AC output and approximately 100kWh of storage across a parallel system using up to three Apex 200 units.

That’s a significant increase over the standalone battery, but your daily consumption still matters. A steady 1kW load uses 24kWh in 24 hours. Heavy-draw appliances can make a large battery feel much smaller.

BLUETTI positions its larger configurations for three to four days of essential-panel backup. How close you get depends on your batteries, appliances, and ability to recharge.

If you want automatic backup through your home’s electrical panel, confirm the compatible transfer equipment, supported circuits, voltage, and output for the exact bundle. Those details determine what you can actually keep running.

Start with your most likely outage, then decide whether you need more runtime, a charging source, or both.

Extra batteries extend runtime. Solar panels or another charging source recharge them. For outages that stretch into days, both can be worth having.

When shopping for a camper van or travel trailer, choosing a battery comes down to more than just capacity. Among its 10 output ports are two connections RV owners will appreciate having built in.

The native 30A TT-30R RV outlet plugs directly into travel trailer shore power inlets for 120V power.

The 12V/30A Anderson port can directly power compatible DC equipment, including portable fridges and communications gear. This avoids converting battery power to AC and then back to DC, cutting out unnecessary conversion steps.

For charging between campsites, the system can pair with the BLUETTI Charger 2, which combines alternator and solar charging support. It lets you use driving time to replenish the battery through faster vehicle alternator charging, then use solar when you’re parked.

BLUETTI’s recommended mobile bundle is the Apex 200 + SORA 500 solar panel + Charger 2. You get storage for camp, solar charging during your stay, and alternator charging on the road. Compatible campground AC gives you another option.

The Apex 200 is the better fit if you value a smaller enclosure, easier transport, native RV ports, and a lower upfront cost. You can start with 2.56kWh and expand to 33.28kWh on one unit, or approximately 100kWh across a fully expanded parallel system.

The Apex 300 is worth considering if your priority is higher native output and capacity for a system that will mostly stay at home. It offers 3,840W of output and 2,764.8Wh of battery storage, and BLUETTI positions it for more advanced home backup, including compatible 120V/240V configurations.

For someone who wants a battery for both blackouts and RV trips, the Apex 200’s size and connections make a useful combination. You can buy the storage you need now and add more when your power needs change.

The Apex 200 launches November 4, with the standalone unit starting at $1,099 during the November 4–18 super early-bird promotion.

Founded in 2013, BLUETTI allows millions of users across more than 120 countries to stay safe and prepared. Its in-house R&D supports a range of solar generators and home backup systems for outage preparation, RV travel, and off-grid living and recreation.

Shop the Apex 200 and launch bundles, and use ELECTREK5OFF at checkout for an extra 5% savings.

#4502. 2026 Tesla Model Y Performance vs. 2027 Rivian R2 Performance Comparison Test

The R2 brings an intuitive, spacious cabin and a classy design, while the Model Y provides handling prowess and impressive near-self-driving capability.

“You come at the king, you best not miss.” That line, uttered menacingly by Michael K. Williams as Omar Little in The Wire, sums up the situation Rivian finds itself in as it launches the R2. The California-based startup broke onto the scene in 2021 with the excellent R1T pickup, and soon after the R1S SUV, but the R2, with its more affordable price point, is the product that could truly solidify Rivian’s place in the market.

To do that, though, Rivian is taking aim at the undisputed king of EVs, the Tesla Model Y, which is the bestselling EV in the United States. Rivian obviously doesn’t expect to overtake the Model Y on the sales charts overnight, but the R2 had better land at least a few punches, because a swing and a miss in the crucial compact SUV segment could see Rivian wind up like Fisker. To assess Rivian’s latest effort, we lined up a 2027 Rivian R2 Performance against a Tesla Model Y Performance in a battle of high-tech, superquick electric SUVs.

See all results for new 2027 Rivian R2 for sale near 08401

While Rivian plans to sell a $46,485 base model starting next year, the R2 launched for the 2027 model year exclusively in the punchy Performance trim. Initial versions come standard with the Launch package, which includes the hands-free driving assistance system and a 4400-pound tow package, which on later R2s will cost $2500 and $950, respectively. The example we drove had the standard setup of all-season tires wrapped around 21-inch wheels, with the only option, $2000 Launch Green paint, bringing the total to $61,485. The boxy newcomer faces off against an EV mainstay in the Model Y. The Performance model we tested had but one option, Full Self-Driving (Supervised), so we tacked on three years’ worth of the $99-per-month subscription, $3564, to come in at $63,194. Tesla fits the Model Y Performance with a trailer hitch as standard, and the sporty SUV can tow up to 3500 pounds.

The R2 and Model Y may be direct competitors, but they take on drastically different shapes. The Model Y features Tesla’s signature egg-like silhouette, and while lesser Model Ys are fairly anonymous looking, the Performance looks pretty sharp in Ultra Red paint with black wheels and trim. The Performance also sports a reshaped front bumper and a small rear lip spoiler.

The R2 is more rectangular, essentially looking like a shrunken version of the R1S. Rivian’s ovoid headlights are more distinctive and affable than the Tesla’s front light bar, which has the menacing look of the eyes on Iron Man’s mask. The R2’s front bumper, with an integrated silver skid plate and tow hooks, hints at the Rivian’s more outdoorsy aura.

The different vibes continue inside, despite both automakers heavily favoring screens over physical controls. In typical Tesla fashion, the Model Y’s interior feels bare, centered around the 16-inch touchscreen. The dashboard, door panels, and center console all have a simple, bland design, although ambient lighting injects a bit of pizzazz. The Performance model’s front seats get more substantial bolstering and a fun “warp speed” badge nestled in below the headrest. Build quality and materials quality have improved greatly since the Model Y’s early days, and carbon-fiber inserts imbue the Performance with a sporty feel. But the materials still aren’t as rich as those in the Rivian—Tesla’s vegan faux leather feels slightly plasticky, and the soft-touch surfaces aren’t as plush.

See all results for new 2027 Rivian R2 for sale near 08401

The R2 looks and feels far more upscale, with a more modern and purposeful design than the austere Tesla. The layered dashboard design is particularly rich: The synthetic leather upper feels like the real deal, tactile wood trim serves as a platform for the touchscreen, and a textured fabric resides below. Hard plastics are well hidden, confined to the lower reaches of the door panels and center console.

In the Tesla, nearly every function, from the climate controls to simply putting the car in drive, is done on the touchscreen, so it’s a relief that Tesla’s display is among the best in the game. The screen is responsive, with an easy-to-read interface. The number of tasks it handles and the amount of information it displays is overwhelming at first, but you quickly learn where the most important functions reside. Still, we prefer physical buttons for things like climate controls, drive modes, and regenerative-braking settings. Shifting between drive and reverse on a screen will always feel a bit odd, and sometimes the Model Y can even shift automatically without any driver input, which is both cool and a little freaky.

Tesla’s infotainment system is absolutely loaded with features, from a built-in dash cam to a web browser and arcade games to pass the time while charging. There’s even Zoom, should you need to pull over to take a meeting, and a Theater app that lets you stream shows and movies while parked. The Model Y also comes with Grok, Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence assistant, and the Toybox, which allows for shenanigans such as turning the seats into whoopee cushions, using the interior camera to transform the car into a photo booth and the exterior speakers to play silly sounds, or making the screen into a virtual sketchpad.

Rivian is also reliant on screens but takes a more traditional approach, complementing the 15.6-inch center touchscreen with an 11.5-inch digital gauge cluster. Rivian’s infotainment is clear and responsive, and the interface feels friendlier than Tesla’s slightly cold digital environment, with a furry, cheerful mascot for the Gear Guard security system and each drive mode accompanied by vivid illustrations. Neither Tesla nor Rivian permit phone mirroring, and while Rivian’s navigation system is beautifully rendered, the map didn’t seem as up to date as the applications we normally use via Apple CarPlay; for example, it thought a recently reopened highway exit was still closed, which Apple Maps and Waze had updated on the day of.

We found Rivian’s dual-screen setup more intuitive. The Model Y’s single-screen approach requires you to glance to the right to check your speed, which doesn’t feel as natural as a quick peek down at the Rivian’s speedometer. Both cars also show a camera view along the side of the car when you activate the turn signal, and once again the Tesla’s setup makes you look away from the road for longer.

The Rivian’s digital controls are joined by unique multifunction thumbwheels on the steering wheel. They can be pushed in and to either side, as well as scrolled, to control a vast array of functions from volume and drive modes to fan speed and temperature. The breadth of functionality is initially daunting, but using the thumbwheels is pretty intuitive, and we only needed a weekend to memorize the controls.

Moving to the rear, the Rivian’s back seat is palatial. The tall roof and flat floor combine for oodles of space for your head and legs, and the low beltline and glass roof create an open, airy feeling. The Tesla, by comparison, feels a bit cramped for taller adults, with notably less legroom. The sloping roofline cuts into headroom and substantially eats into cargo space. In our testing, we were able to load 10 carry-on suitcases into the Rivian’s rear cargo hold but only seven in the Model Y. The R2 can also roll down its rear glass into the liftgate, just like a Toyota 4Runner.

Tesla makes up for its less spacious back seat by treating rear passengers to their own 8.0-inch touchscreen. The display can not only adjust the heated seats, climate control system, and the audio, but also can be used to play games or stream video. The R2’s rear occupants get a simpler console with air vents and buttons for the heated seats. Both SUVs provide rear passengers with a pair of USB-C ports, with Rivian hiding them in the front seatbacks.

Both SUVs pack dual-motor, all-wheel-drive powertrains. The R2 Performance’s permanent-magnet motors churn out 656 horsepower and 609 pound-feet of torque, and the R2 can decouple the 294-hp front motor via a clutch in the differential. Most of the time the R2 runs in rear-wheel drive, until the rear wheels slip or you demand more performance than the 362-hp rear motor can muster. The Model Y’s powertrain, with an induction motor up front and a permanent-magnet motor at the rear, packs a bit less oomph at 510 horsepower.

Despite the 146-hp gap between the two SUVs, the R2 and Model Y posted remarkably similar numbers at the test track. The Model Y zips to 60 mph in 3.3 seconds with the R2 just two-tenths behind, and the two electric SUVs are neck and neck by the time they reach 80 mph. At the quarter-mile, the Rivian edges in front, completing the run in 11.4 seconds at 126 mph, one-tenth ahead of the Tesla and 4 mph faster. While the R2 tops out at 130 mph, the Model Y keeps going to 153 mph. Both are mega-quick for five-seat SUVs.

The Model Y has a slight advantage in our passing-acceleration test from 30 to 50 mph at 1.6 seconds versus 1.8 seconds for the Rivian, but the R2 is two-tenths quicker from 50 to 70 mph, clocking that jump in 2.1 seconds.

While the acceleration times are extremely similar—and, again, astonishingly swift for five-seat SUVs—the Model Y clearly wins the top-speed race by 20-plus mph.

Things are just as close when it comes to slowing down. Slam on the brakes at 70 mph, and the Tesla comes to a halt in 179 feet; the Rivian needs 178. When stopping from 100 mph, the Model Y holds a six-foot advantage.

HIGHS: Lots of room inside, sophisticated and upscale design, good ride and handling balance.LOWS: Noisy suspension, overly strong regen braking, more power than it can use in the corners.VERDICT: Rivian comes out swinging with a well-designed SUV that drives well and is easy to live with.

The less powerful Model Y’s ability to essentially match the R2’s performance is due in part to its lower curb weight. The Tesla tipped the scales at 4438 pounds, with the Rivian hauling around an extra 547 pounds. This discrepancy also contributes to a big difference on the skidpad. The Rivian, riding on Pirelli Scorpion MS Elect tires, posted 0.81 g, while the Tesla, shod in Hankook Ion Evo AS SUV tires, managed 0.88 g.

We also tested an R2 on the 20-inch wheels and BFGoodrich Trail-Terrain T/A+ tires; it was a tenth quicker to 60 mph and through the quarter-mile. In a surprise twist, the R2 on all-terrain tires also delivered significantly better braking performance, stopping from 70 mph in 166 feet and from 100 mph in 340 feet. Even roadholding improved to 0.84 g.

Numbers don’t tell the full story, however, and the Model Y Performance and R2 Performance feel vastly different from behind the wheel. On a curvy back road, the Tesla is much sportier. It turns in eagerly, the tires provide plenty of grip, and the body stays flat and poised. While the steering isn’t communicative, it is accurate, and the whole package feels taut and agile. The Model Y Performance also feels extremely quick in Insane mode, with a launch befitting the warp-speed badge Tesla sticks on the back. The cornering prowess comes with a trade-off, however. The Tesla pairs adaptive dampers with a coil-spring suspension, and even in the softer Standard setting, the ride is stiff, with every bump transmitted into the cabin. It may be an improvement over the previous Model Y Performance, but the ride is still quite firm.

The Rivian is incredibly zippy in Sport mode, but it doesn’t encourage you to push in the corners the way the Tesla does. The nose points upward when you floor the go-pedal, and there’s more body roll than in the Tesla. The R2 ends up feeling a bit nervous when trying to accelerate forcefully out of a corner. Still, the steering is precise, and the Rivian handles competently, but it instills less confidence in using the full extent of its 656 horsepower in anything other than a straight line.

In normal driving, both the Rivian and the Tesla move briskly and assertively. The Rivian, which also uses coil springs and adaptive dampers, rides noticeably better around town. Although the R2 doesn’t exactly gloss over bumps, impacts are far less intrusive than in the Tesla, as long as you avoid the Firm damper setting. The R2’s suspension can be noisy over rougher pavement, however, and at highway speeds the thunks are accompanied by the rush of wind around the upright A-pillars. At 70 mph, we recorded 67 decibels in the R2’s cabin, one more than in the Model Y. That boxier shape, however, makes for excellent visibility; the Tesla, by contrast, has a tiny slot of a rear window, although the way the Tesla’s nose dips downward provides an expansive view ahead.

HIGHS: Nimble handling, packed with features, Full Self-Driving is getting seriously good.LOWS: It feels like they forgot to finish designing the cabin, ride can be jarring, roofline compromises interior space.VERDICT: The Model Y provides a high-tech, modern experience, but one that’s coldly efficient.

Neither SUV lets you switch regenerative braking fully off. Rivian’s lowest setting is still quite strong, so you’d better like one-pedal driving. Tesla offers two regen braking settings: Standard is quite strong, while Reduced felt like the perfect balance, far less strong than the R2’s weakest setting.

The Rivian is more able to venture off the beaten path. We didn’t take the R2 on anything more challenging than a dirt road, but its 9.6 inches of ground clearance—only one-tenth less than a Jeep Wrangler Sport—and solid approach and departure angles should give owners the confidence to travel farther down the trailhead than the Model Y, with its carlike 6.4 inches of ground clearance.

We also have to talk about, well, not driving. For years, one of Tesla’s unique selling points has been its Full Self-Driving system, and it only gets more impressive each year. While many automakers now offer hands-free driving systems for use on highways, Tesla’s stands out for its ability to take you door to door with zero input required beyond simply plugging in the address; the car takes off, navigating you there swiftly and mostly confidently, even parking at the final destination. Still, we’re not sure FSD really needs a Mad Max setting that allows it to drive up to 85 mph, and we remain unconvinced about using a camera-only system in rain or snow.

Rivian’s Autonomy+ hands-free driving feature isn’t as comprehensive. It doesn’t currently work with the navigation system, but Rivian is planning to add point-to-point capability next year. Currently, it’s best suited to highway driving, where it performs adequately but cautiously. Unlike GM’s latest Super Cruise, Autonomy+ doesn’t automatically change lanes when you come up behind slower traffic, and when you do initiate a lane change via the turn signal stalk, it isn’t the smoothest, getting over quickly with an abrupt steering movement. Even within a lane, it feels a bit more nervous that the Tesla’s system, making many small adjustments in order to stay in between the lines.

The R2 Performance packs an 88-kWh lithium-ion battery, and the EPA estimates 330 miles of range on the 21-inch wheels, with the 20-inch wheels dropping that figure to 307 miles. On our 75-mph highway range test, the R2 maxed out at 260 miles, but the smaller wheels and all-terrain tires slashed range to just 220 miles. The Model Y Performance has 81 kWh of battery capacity, earning a 306-mile range estimate from the EPA. Still, the Tesla managed to beat the Rivian in Car and Driver testing, eking out 270 miles in the 75-mph highway test.

Neither SUV has much of an advantage when it comes to charging. The R2 can hit a peak charging rate of 230 kilowatts, and in our DC fast-charging test, it needed 39 minutes to get from 10 to 90 percent, averaging 119 kilowatts. The Model Y maxes out at 250 kilowatts, and while we weren’t able to test the fast-charging of this Performance trim, a different 2026 Model Y we tested went from 10 to 90 percent in 44 minutes. The R2 is also capable of bidirectional charging, allowing it to power external electronic devices, something this Tesla cannot do.

The battle between the R2 and Model Y is incredibly close. The performance figures are nearly identical, and both SUVs provide adequate range and similar charging speeds. Those who want to carve up back roads will be drawn toward the Model Y’s agility, and Tesla’s Full Self-Driving system remains unmatched. But when it comes to living with the car, the R2’s more compliant ride, more spacious and luxurious cabin, and superior interior ergonomics won us over. While we love crisp driving dynamics as much as anyone, we think the R2 better accomplishes the mission of what a compact SUV should be. The Tesla remains a great option in a crowded segment, but the R2 is coming for the throne.

#4501. This Startup Is Turning Used E-Bike Batteries Into Affordable Energy Storage

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Millions of e-bike and e-scooter batteries are thrown away every year, even though they might still have life in them. Now, a German startup is trying to reduce battery waste by integrating used batteries from e-mobility vehicles into energy storage systems.

EDENenergy, which has just three part-time staff members in addition to its three founders, has shipped its first commercial product, a 70-kilowatt-hour battery system that uses no fewer than 112 second-life e-scooter batteries.

All modules were thoroughly tested, and the results were better than expected. The company’s founders, who used to be researchers at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, said that they expected the old batteries to have roughly 80% life left in them, but the tests revealed that most retained about 90% of their original capacity.

After being abused in their previous life, the e-scooter batteries will have a much easier future in the startup’s energy storage systems, where vibrations and large temperature fluctuations are non-existent. What’s more, the long-term energy capacity of the system can be easily kept at 70 kWh by simply replacing modules that become unusable down the line.

The startup said it remotely monitors each module, and when it’s time for a replacement, it can be done without powering down the whole system. That’s a big plus, especially for energy-sensitive scenarios where cutting the power would result in massive losses.

The keen-eyed among you might have noticed that there’s a solar inverter on one side of the battery box. That’s because EDENenergy’s first product was designed for companies that have solar panels but can’t store solar energy yet. “In mid-October, we delivered the first storage system to a customer, which was an important milestone for our young company,” said Florian Bierwirth, one of the founders. “With this storage size, we initially aim to target medium-sized companies in the region that have a photovoltaic system but do not yet have a storage solution.”

For its next step, the startup wants to come up with a way of using different batteries from different manufacturers. “To do this, the connector interfaces, battery management system, and communication protocols must be adapted for each new battery. There’s a particularly wide range of options when it comes to e-bikes,” said Bierwirth. Currently, the small company relies on large suppliers that can send in large numbers of the same battery type.

A larger-capacity battery system of up to 300 kWh is also in the works, putting roughly 500 second-life e-scooter modules to good use instead of sending them to the landfill. The batteries will eventually give up, but when that happens, they’ll be sent to a recycling facility where they’ll be dismantled, and their contents will be reused, if possible.
