#4500. Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.

Technically, it has pedals. You can pedal it fairly effectively too, with the actually adjustable seat. You can even pedal it for fun, which is more than I can say for some of the increasingly motorcycle-shaped “e-bikes” I’ve tested lately.

But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US. Not when we’re talking about dual motors producing up to 6,000W of peak power and speeds of around 45 mph.

And you know what? That’s fine. As long as we’re all honest about what this thing is.

The Aniioki A9 Pro Max is absolutely massive, and the spec sheet makes that abundantly clear.

The version I tested uses a pair of 2,500W direct-drive hub motors, one in each wheel, with Aniioki claiming 3,000W peak power from each motor. That gives the bike a combined peak figure of 6,000W and up to 250 Nm of combined torque. It’s hard to overstate how massive that is.

Then there’s the battery. You can choose between a 60V 70Ah pack with 4.2 kWh of capacity or an even larger 60V 80Ah pack packing 4.8 kWh. For comparison, many typical commuter e-bikes have somewhere around 500-700 Wh of battery. The smaller battery here is roughly six to eight times that size. That’s absolutely in the territory of legit light electric motorcycles.

Aniioki claims up to 230+ miles (370 km) of pedal-assist range, though as usual, you should take maximum e-bike range figures as best-case numbers. Using the throttle and enjoying those big motors is going to dramatically reduce that figure. Even so, with more than 4 kWh of battery underneath you, range anxiety isn’t exactly the first thing that comes to mind.

All that hardware comes with a predictable penalty: weight. The 70Ah model tips the scales at around 188 lb (85 kg), while the 80Ah version approaches 193 lb (87.5 kg). Those aren’t e-bike weights. Those are motorcycle weights. Again, you can see the direction this is going.

Here’s where the A9 Pro Max gets more interesting to me.

A lot of high-powered e-motos include pedals seemingly as a regulatory fig leaf. They’re technically there, but the geometry is so bad that nobody in their right mind would want to pedal the thing farther than across a parking lot. Even some smaller and presumably Class 2 legal e-bikes that have moto-style frames are nearly unpedalable for actual riding over any reasonable distance.

But the A9 here is actually pedalable thanks to having something that more closely resembles a bicycle seat, plus adjustability that lets riders dial in the correct seat height.

The A9 Pro Max feels more like a strange combination of an oversized fat-tire e-bike and a small electric motorcycle. There’s a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain and a huge 72-tooth chainring, meaning the pedals aren’t entirely ornamental.

I actually enjoyed pedaling it with the pedal assist engaged. You’re obviously not going to mistake a nearly 200-pound machine rolling on enormous 26 x 4.8-inch tires for a lightweight fitness bike, but there’s something fun about contributing some human power while two giant hub motors do most of the heavy lifting.

And when you don’t feel like pedaling, there’s a full-twist throttle waiting for you.

That combination is really the appeal here. You can ride it more like an e-bike when the mood strikes, or twist the throttle and treat it more like a lightweight e-moto.

And again, I don’t want to beat a dead horse here, but remember: the pedals don’t make this an electric bicycle. It’s still an e-moto, but it’s one that you can actually have fun pedaling. You can treat it like a mech suit, where pedaling translates into crazy power, as if you have super-human legs. And with the insanely large 72t chainring, pedaling at higher speeds is actually doable. Though I’ll tell you right now, pedaling at 40 mph (64 km/h) is not exactly a normal or natural feeling.

And it’s worth pointing out that at a starting price of US $2,899 (or more for the larger battery capacities), that’s a fairly reasonable price compared to most e-motos that can be more limiting in how and where you can ride them.

Fortunately, Aniioki seems to understand that putting this much power on two wheels requires more serious components than the average bicycle.

The braking setup is particularly wild. There are two massive 300mm brake rotors on the front wheel and another 300mm rotor out back, along with a linked CBS braking system. The front uses custom eight-piston calipers (the pair of quad-piston calipers) while the rear gets a custom six-piston setup.

There’s also an adjustable air-suspension fork with 110mm of travel, rear suspension to smooth out bumps at higher speeds, integrated lighting and turn signals, and a large five-inch display that even incorporates features like Bluetooth audio and a recording camera.

That brings us to the elephant in the room.

In the US, consumer-product rules generally define a low-speed electric bicycle around a motor of less than 750W and a maximum motor-powered speed below 20 mph (32 km/h), while individual states use their own operating laws that typically match the familiar Class 1/2/3 framework. A 6,000W machine capable of around 45 mph (72 km/h) blows straight through normal limits.

So please don’t see pedals and assume this belongs on your local bicycle path.

Where and how you can legally operate something like the A9 Pro Max depends on your local laws and whether it can qualify under another vehicle category. For many owners, the sensible place to enjoy its full performance is going to be private property or other areas where such vehicles are permitted.

That caveat doesn’t make the bike itself bad. It just means buyers need to understand what they’re buying.

And judged on what it actually is rather than what the word “e-bike” on the product page suggests, I had a lot of fun on it.

There are certainly riders who would look at a nearly 200-pound, 45 mph machine and say, “Why not just buy an electric motorcycle?” That’s a perfectly reasonable question.

In addition to kW power limits, the legal boundary for what is an e-bike should also include weight. Anything over 100lbs including battery is no longer an e-bike and it carries a dangerous amount of momentum once it is cruising. 190 lbs is ridiculous.

But I also understand the appeal of this weird middle ground. The A9 Pro Max retains enough bicycle DNA that you can pedal it around and enjoy pedal assist, yet has enough battery and motor underneath you to deliver something much closer to small-motorcycle performance when you twist the throttle.

Imagine going off-road and getting to fly up hills while pedaling hard, but then being able to switch to throttle once your legs get worn out. Sure, it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s a cup of tea.

This bike is big. It’s heavy. It’s absurdly powerful by e-bike standards. And it absolutely isn’t the machine I’d recommend for someone looking for a normal street-legal electric bicycle.

But if what you actually want is a big, powerful electric two-wheeler that still lets you turn the pedals when the mood strikes, the Aniioki A9 Pro Max makes a surprisingly compelling argument for this increasingly bizarre category of pedal-equipped e-motos.

#4499. This V-16 Resurrects a Forgotten Engine Architecture for a Custom Build

Most things in life come down to timing, including dialing in the firing order of a V-16 made from two LS3 V-8s.

“If you have two V-8s that are exactly in the same timing, your pistons aren’t firing properly; it can rip itself apart—not good.” That’s Bryan Fuller summarizing the challenges presented by physically joining a pair of LS3 V-8 engines to create an 854 cubic-inch V-16 reported to make in the neighborhood of 1200 horsepower.

But while getting 16 holes to fire in a complementary, non-destructive manner is a feat unto itself, the impetus behind the project is a one-off custom Roadster designed by Hot Wheels with direct input from the unnamed, ostensibly well-heeled client. Fuller says the design of the 19.5-foot-long custom roadster is inspired by the 1938 Cadillac V-16 Series-90, but devotees of the brand’s history will recognize the spirit of the 1937 Cadillac V16 Hartmann Cabriolet, a two-off run of vehicles crafted in Switzerland for—you guessed it—a wealthy client.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07430

Back in the 21st century, Fuller had to address the timing, cooling, fuel, and air issues, as well as engineer their structural unity and their combined output to ensure the V-8s play nicely together.

As for ignition timing, the rear engine is clocked back “about 45 degrees,” which allows the tandem V-8s to fire in the proper order of a V-16. A single starter spins both. The mating of the torque is achieved by mounting a giubo joint (a.k.a. flex disc), a flex joint comprised of a rubber or urethane center with metal mounting plates on either side that mates the rear of the front engine with the front of the rear engine. Structural connection of the V-8s is made via a trio of CNC-machined plates, one in the center valley and one each on the lower right and left sides.

Ignition is handled traditionally, with two computers and individual plug wires, Fuller noted that “the LS3 is a known quantity,” and years of tuning the LS3 V-8 makes the job a little easier. Cooling is the only shared major system. A Meziere water pump generates enough pressure to move the coolant through both engines, out a custom dual outlet, and into a single radiator. Air is handled by a highly modified Holley intake that will continue to be modified as the project moves to installing the powertrain in the body.

The Tremec T-56 Magnum transmission was optimized by Bowler Performance Transmissions, who polished the internals, among other tweaks. As expected, ARP hardware is utilized throughout the project. Even the powertrain table it sits on is custom-built.

See all results for used cars for sale near 07430

At this point, the V-16 is waiting for the Roadster Shop to finish the custom chassis so the team can begin the process of combining all three elements to create a fully operational vehicle. How long that process will take is unclear, but the V-16 makes a pretty nice conversation piece just as it sits on its custom display stand.

#4498. DeepWay electric semi arrives in New Zealand, and gets a new name

New Zealand’s Foodstuffs North Island Limited has given its latest electric semi truck an electrifying new identity, courtesy of a second-grade student at a local elementary school.

The Chinese-built DeepWay Star began delivering chilled and frozen groceries across New Zealand’s lower North Island earlier this year – and, after a naming competition organized with students at Russell Street School in Palmerston North, the big HD EV has got a new name: Evie.

The winning name came from Year 2 (read: second grade) student named Madison, who beat out suggestions including Buzzy Bee, Lightning, and Bolt. Madison got to officially unveil the truck’s new name alongside her classmates, local officials and Foodstuffs representatives.

“Our trucks are out on the road every day delivering food to stores and communities, so we thought it would be great to get the kids involved and give our first electric truck a bit of personality,” explains Foodstuffs North Island General Manager Supply Chain, Yang Zhang. “There were some brilliant ideas, but Evie was a pretty fitting name for an EV. The best part is knowing Madison and the other students will be able to spot Evie out on the road and know they played a part in it.”

Madison was allowed to do the unveiling honors, revealing Evie’s new name alongside her other classmates, Palmerston North’s Mayor, Grant Smith, local MP Tangi Utikeri, and local PAK’nSAVE, New World, and Four Square grocers who will be receiving deliveries from Evie.

In its first few months on the road, Evie’s travelled nearly 45,000 kilometers (~28,000 miles) and avoided more than 81,000 kg of harmful carbon emissions – which the company claims is roughly equivalent to taking 35 ICE cars off the road for a full year.

As for the truck itself, it has a sort of Tesla-ish, anteater-y look, and significantly longer range than the StarWay, offering more than 500 km (~310 miles) of range from its 600 kWh CATL-built LFP battery packs that can plug into charge ports two at a time for lickety-quick charging in about 30 minutes. If that’s too long of a wait, the Star can swap its tired batteries for fresh ones in special battery-sway stations in just six minutes.

The DeepWay’s electric motors put out 491 kW (~660 hp) of power, and a positively tectonic 75,000 (!) Nm (~55,000 lb-ft) (!!) of torque – more than enough to get the 50 tons (100,000 lb.) of GVWR it’s rated for up to speed.

It is great to see electric trucks replacing Diesel. I just can’t understand why EV adoption is so slow to take off in New Zealand. It has plenty of great low cost EVs and petrol is all imported and expensive.

You can check out the pictures, above, then let us know what you think of the big Chinese BEV and it’s fun new name in the comments.

#4497. EVs Made Up Nearly A Third Of UK Sales As Europe's Electric Boom Continues

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

While EV sales are growing slowly in the U.S., despite the loss of federal tax incentives, they're exploding in the UK. According to UK's car industry lobby New Automotive, 49,155 new fully battery-electric vehicles (BEV) were sold in October. That's not only a massive 54% increase over last October, but it's 32% of the UK's new car market share, or almost a third.

That 32% market share also gave EVs the largest market share of any one fuel type, more than gas, diesel, or hybrids. "Almost one in three new cars sold in October was fully electric, more than any other fuel type, and electric car sales are up by more than half on last year," said Ben Nelmes, CEO at New AutoMotive. "Drivers are voting with their wallets. Every one of those new electric cars means a household spending less on running costs, and a country less exposed to the oil price shock."

There's more EV variety in the UK than there is in America. The UK has access to EVs from brands like Renault, Peugeot, Fiat, Volkswagen, Skoda, and even Chinese EVs like BYD and Jaecoo. Last month, Kia, BMW, Volkswagen, and BYD led the country's electric market. Tesla slumped after a big September.

Year-to-date, though, Tesla is number one, with 9.53% market share. That's up 25.4% from last year, too. Kia took second place, with 6.9% market share, and BYD came in third, with 6.8%. What's surprising is that no European EV brands were in the top three, despite being in their home continent. I'd sell a non-essential organ for a Renault 5 E-Tech, so I'm surprised to see cars like that not taking top spots in the UK.

It isn't just new EVs, either. The UK is also seeing a jump in used EVs, just like we are here. According to EV Powered, data shows that more and more UK customers are shopping for used EVs.

The run up in oil costs is driving record EV sales across Europe. BEVs took 37% share of the car market in Germany, the country's road traffic agency said, with over 94,000 vehicles sold. That's a nearly 80% increase year over year.

#4496. BMW Alpina’s First Production Car Glides During High-Speed Testing

The car will be an elevated approach to the 7-series sedan featuring Alpina’s iconic 20-spoke wheels and quad-oval exhaust pipes.

BMW is testing its first production model under its new BMW Alpina subbrand, and Alpina’s original mantra rings clear through the camouflage in the automaker’s sneak peek. While it’ll be a high-speed beast, the goal is to deliver an incredibly smooth ride.

Alpina began as a German tuner company in the early 1960s that specialized in high-performance engines with the ultimate comfortable cabin. Rather than outfitting BMWs to attack tracks, Alpina built cars that glided on pavement and wrapped drivers in luxury materials. BMW recently took control of the company and re-established it as a subbrand, much like Mercedes-Maybach.

See all results for used BMW Alpina for sale near 95134

We reported early this year that the first BMW Alpina production car would likely be inspired by the 7-series. Then, in May, the automaker unveiled the Vision BMW Alpina concept, which was said to be inspiration for the upcoming model. New photos and videos of the prototype Alpina show strong 7-series bones, with the build taking on more of a standard sedan silhouette than the concept’s smooth, sweeping rear end.

No Alpina is complete without its signature 20-spoke wheels, and BMW says the upcoming model takes the light alloy rollers to the next level by wrapping them in specially developed tires with a layer of foam inside for a smoother ride. Talk about bougie.

Tech specs are still few and far between, and the only thing BMW has confirmed in terms of performance is that the Alpina will be powered by a V-8. A video from BMW shows the car reaching over 186 mph during high-speed testing in Italy. Since this isn’t a track-focused model, the exterior lacks some of the aero bits that would normally accompany a faster, more expensive BMW. Instead, most of the Alpina’s standout exterior qualities are found in the rear, where quad-oval exhaust pipes and a small spoiler break up the standard 7-series’s body lines.

Based on the video below, the interior looks pretty similar to the 7-series, with a thin panoramic display and two screens along the dashboard. It gets the same four-spoke steering wheel as the 7-series, but the seats seem to be a bit different than the stock option, and it’s likely the cabin will be dressed in upgraded materials.

The ultra-luxury sedan will be the first to roll out under BMW Alpina, and it’s expected to arrive sometime next year. BMW hasn’t said what else is on the horizon for the brand, though it’s likely the three-row BMW X7 SUV will be the next to get Alpina treatment.

#4495. Electric cars are about to overtake petrol in the UK, data shows

Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK’s new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That’s the closest the two have been.

At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December.

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market.

All of that growth came from plug-ins. BEV registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%.

Through the first 10 months of the year, the UK has now registered 503,805 BEVs, up 30.4%, for a 26.6% market share. Petrol’s year-to-date share is down to 41.1%, from 47.2% at the same point last year.

We pulled SMMT’s monthly fuel-type data going back to March 2024 to see where this is heading. Note that SMMT counts mild hybrids as petrol (or diesel) in its headline categories, and that’s generally how we count them at Electrek.

In March 2024, petrol held 55.9% of the market and BEVs 15.2%. In October 2026, it was 37.2% vs 32.0%. Petrol’s share is shrinking by about half a point per month on a linear trend, while BEVs gain about 0.36 points a month. Extend both lines and they cross around August 2027 at roughly 33% each.

But that’s the slow scenario, because it ignores December.

UK BEV share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their ZEV Mandate targets. BEVs hit 31.0% in December 2024 and 32.2% in December 2025, when petrol was at 39.4%. Over the last five months, BEV share has run about 5 points higher than a year earlier, and petrol about 7 points lower. If December follows that pattern, BEVs land around 37% and petrol around 32%.

That would be the first time BEVs beat petrol in SMMT’s headline numbers, mild hybrids included.

However, SMMT’s own forecast of 27.2% BEV share for the full year implies roughly 31% for November and December combined, which would make it a much closer call. And on a stricter definition that puts mild hybrids with hybrids instead of petrol, BEVs already outsold every other powertrain in August.

Zoom out to full years and the picture is just as clear. Cars that run only on petrol or diesel, mild hybrids included, made up 72.5% of the UK market in 2021. This year, they’re at 45.5%.

None of this is good enough for the SMMT, which is using the release to push the government, again, to cut the ZEV Mandate targets.

The mandate requires 33% of 2026 sales to be zero-emission. SMMT now forecasts 27.2%. It expects 32% next year against a 38% target, and 37.5% in 2028 against 52%, a 14.5-point gap.

The trade group says automakers have spent “billions” on discounts, 0% financing, deposit contributions, and even subsidized charging to move EVs, on top of the government’s Electric Car Grant. It also slammed last week’s Budget, which confirmed a new EV-specific road tax (eVED) starting in 2028 and kept 20% VAT on public charging.

“Higher targets may force supply, but they do not create demand,” SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said.

We’ve heard this one before. The SMMT made the same argument after September’s record 99,199 BEV registrations, and the government already opened a review of the mandate this year.

This might be the main reason why the trade group wants to slow things down. The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.

Tesla, on the other hand, registered just 282 cars in October, down 45% from 511 a year ago. The first month of the quarter is always slow for Tesla in the UK, and the brand is still up 31% year-to-date at 46,526 units after a big September. But it didn’t have a single model in October’s top 10 BEVs, which was led by the Skoda Enyaq (1,568), Mini Countryman (1,494), and Jaecoo 5 (1,465).

The SMMT’s framing is that there’s a “demand gap.” The data shows the opposite. BEV registrations are up 30% this year while petrol is shrinking every single month. That’s not a market rejecting EVs.

The SMMT is not a neutral organisation, they have been briefing against EVs for years and continue to do so.

The ZEV mandate is NOT a measure of how many pure BEVs are sold, and the SMMT know it, it's a measure of REDUCING emission against a level set in the past.

Those emissions reductions can be met by selling BEVs, or selling more efficient PHEVs or even selling more efficient petrol or diesel cars! The manufacturers can also buy credits if they choose to.

NO manufacturer has paid any ZEV fines to date (DfT announcement March 2026)

As for the "heavy discounts" and "loss making sales", well I have two data points on that.

1. The retail price of EVs has continued to climb in the UK over the past 6 years, despite the cost of any average 50kWh battery pack dropping several thousand dollars.

2. There are hundreds of main dealerships who are buying cars from the manufacturers, driving them for the minimum 3 month period, often with just a few thousand miles on the clock and then selling them with a 30-35% retail price discount, and then repeating ad infinitum. The dealerships are still making a few thousand with each transaction, so we know where the manufacturers price really sits.

And the discounts automakers keep complaining about? That’s the mandate doing exactly what it was designed to do. It forces automakers to sell EVs, so they price them to sell, and buyers respond. Hawes says targets don’t create demand, but cheaper EVs clearly do. October proves it.

Now, is the jump to 52% in 2028 steep? It is steep, but it looks achievable to me. If anything is hurting demand, it’s the government’s own moves: a new EV-only road tax and 20% VAT on public charging. That’s what the industry should be fighting. It’s too early for that.

Either way, petrol’s days as the UK’s default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Our bet is December.

#4494. China Has An Iron Grip On EV Batteries. Here's America’s Plan To Break It

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

The U.S. Department of Energy last week released a new three-step plan to localize the supply chain of batteries and reduce America’s reliance on China. The plan may not even mention electric vehicles, but the EV market could be among its biggest beneficiaries if successfully executed.

Citing data from research firm BloombergNEF, the DOE said demand for batteries would increase four fold between 2025 and 2035, from 179 gigawatt-hours to 707 GWh. The demand is expected to skyrocket across sectors including transportation, the power grid, AI data centers, consumer electronics, and drones.

While the report acknowledged that America’s battery cell and pack manufacturing had improved over the past few years, the core supply chain was still heavily reliant on imports. That means things like raw material mining and the production of a battery’s subcomponents such as anodes, cathodes, electrolytes, and separators were still largely happening overseas, mostly in China.

To fix this, DOE said a new three-step plan was necessary, and the following are its objectives:

In part one of this plan, the focus would be to invest in the battery supply chain. “DOE is prioritizing investments to shift from a discontinuous, import-reliant supply chain to an integrated domestic production system through the upstream (mining), midstream (refining and engineered materials), and downstream (cells, packs, and end products),” the DOE said. It added that it would focus on targeted investments in companies that specialize in extraction, recycling, refining, and equipment manufacturing.

Part two outlines developing and commercializing next-generation batteries that are right for their specific applications. “These batteries should be more affordable, longer lasting, higher performing, and less reliant on critical minerals in select market segments,” the DOE said. So think solid-state cells or more advanced versions of current lithium-ion technology. And the final part of the plan is to get them past the “valley of death,” meaning converting discoveries made in the lab into actual products people can buy.

To be clear, the Biden administration had shared similar objectives back in 2021 in far more detail with a focus on clean energy, social justice, and equitable jobs. The Trump administration’s blueprint is much thinner and instead leans on national security, the grid, humanoid robots, and the enormous power demands of AI data centers. It doesn't explicitly mention EVs, but instead says next-gen batteries would also help in the transportation sector.

It's also worth remembering that America's battery industry was surging long before that. After Trump swept to power in 2024, battery manufacturing in the U.S. took a severe hit. According to clean energy think tank E2, the U.S. canceled, closed or downsized battery projects worth $42 billion between 2022 and 2026, costing the nation over 85,000 jobs. Across the broader clean energy sector, the sum increases to $137 billion, costing over 240,000 jobs, according to the same report.

The new blueprint is still a step in the right direction, even if it is more of a continued effort. It also reflects how much the battery landscape has changed since the start of the decade. EV sales have been up and down, while demand for stationary energy storage has surged, driven by utility upgrades and AI data centers. The revised strategy accounts for that shift, and automakers could still benefit over the long term for their EV plans.

#4492. Car Body Styles and Sizes Explained, from Compact Sedans to Full-Size SUVs and Everything in Between

If you’re looking understand the difference between a coupe and a sedan, or even between a compact SUV and a mid-size SUV, let us break it down.

The term "body style" is an all-encompassing label used to describe the size, shape, and characteristics of a vehicle. For example, sedans and pickup trucks are two popular vehicle body styles in the United States. At Car and Driver, we separate vehicles into eight primary body styles, making them easier to categorize (and easier for you to shop).

Within those eight broad body styles are a host of different variations that get even more specific. Size is one of the most important distinctions. We typically categorize vehicles in the following sizes, listed in increasing order: subcompact, compact, mid-size, and full-size. There are also differences in luxury vehicles versus non-luxury vehicles, and some vehicles that defy categorization altogether. Not sure where the car you’re interested in fits? We've broken down all of the main vehicle types and their subcategories to help you understand the body style basics.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405

Sedans are what most people picture when they think of a traditional passenger car. Sedans have four doors and incorporate a three-box design (jargon for a design with a distinct hood, passenger compartment, and trunk). Sedans come in multiple types and sizes, ranging from fuel-efficient and small compact to luxurious and large full-size options.

The smallest sedans in the U.S. are subcompact in size. Among non-luxury options, there are no sedans remaining in this segment, as automakers have dropped these entry-level options. The luxury subcompact segment is more flush with options. This subset includes the Audi A3 and Mercedes CLA-class.

Compact sedans are larger than subcompacts but smaller than mid-size models. Both mainstream and luxury options abound. In either form, compacts tend to offer reasonable space for cargo and people, though taller individuals may find these models’ rear seat room a bit too confining. The Honda Civic is a benchmark of the mainstream compact segment, as it expertly blends a reasonably roomy rear seat and trunk with enjoyable driving dynamics for a reasonable price. It’s why the model’s practically a regular on our 10Best Cars.

Mid-size sedans tend to sacrifice some of the driving enjoyment of their compact kin for additional rear seat and cargo space. These machines are perfect for those who regularly carry passengers or haul various items. The best mid-size sedans afford this extra versatility with only a marginal hit to behind-the-wheel joy. This includes the 10Best-winning Honda Accord in the mainstream segment and vehicles such as the BMW 5-series in the mid-size luxury segment.

Full-size sedans these days are the flagship models in a brand’s lineup. Only luxury-badged full-size sedans remain, as previous mainstream full-size options such as the Ford Taurus were discontinued years ago. The luxurious Mercedes-Benz S-class is a prime example of the category. Such sedans tend to emphasize a comfortable ride and loads of rear seat space above all else.

See all results for used cars for sale near 29405

Sports sedans come in subcompact, compact, mid-size, and full-size forms. These models tend to be high-performance variants of more run-of-the-mill models, though some may argue that a number of these “run-of-the-mill” options are sports sedans in and of themselves. For instance, the subcompact Cadillac CT4 and compact Cadillac CT5 feature engaging rear-drive dynamics that arguably make these sedans worthy of the title. However, we limit the sports sedan designation to the models' truly sporty 10Best-winning CT4-V Blackwing and CT5-V Blackwing variants.

Sport utility vehicles, better known as SUVs, are the most popular vehicle type in the United States. This is in large part due to their versatility. Most SUVs offer generous space in the cabin and cargo area. They’re also offered in a variety of forms, from wagon-like crossover SUVs to hardcore off-road ones. Some are even capable of holding their own on the track.

Subcompact SUVs are the smallest of the breed. These typically inexpensive SUVs (relatively speaking, of course) often offer middling room for rear seat passengers or cargo, but do include the higher seating position and extra ground clearance that SUVs are associated with. Like their sedan stablemates, these models are available in both mainstream and luxury guises. While some subcompact SUVs feel more like penalty boxes, others, such as the 10Best-winning Chevrolet Trax, do a great job of making these entry-level machines feel anything but.

Compact SUVs—for example, the 10Best-winning Honda CR-V,—are effectively modern-day station wagons, combining reasonable rear seat and cargo space with a manageably sized footprint. Most mainstream compact SUVs are relatively affordable, and the best examples offer a versatile interior in a reasonably fun-to-drive package. On the other end of the spectrum, the 10Best-winning Porsche Macan trades interior space and versatility for dynamics that rival those of the best sports cars. In between sit luxury compact SUVs like the Genesis GV70, which combine luxurious wares with a comfortable ride and a generally playful chassis for once the roads start to turn.

Mid-size SUVs often have more passenger and cargo space. They also tend to offer a more premium feel, though both mainstream and luxury options are available. Some mid-size models offer just two rows of seats; while these choices offer the same five-passenger seating capacity as compact SUVs in most cases they have more space behind the rear seats for cargo when compared with a compact SUV. A prime example of a two-row, mid-size SUV is the Honda Passport.

Many mid-size SUVs are available with three rows of seats, providing seating for six, seven, or eight passengers depending on the configuration. The 10Best-winning Kia Telluride exemplifies the mid-size three-row category.

Full-size SUVs take advantage of their substantial dimensions, providing generous space for passengers and their stuff, as well as formidable towing capabilities. General Motors' Chevrolet Tahoe and GMC Yukon are two notable examples.

Crossover SUVs are available in all shapes and sizes, and many of the models we’ve already discussed are categorized as crossovers. Unlike traditional SUVs, which ride on truck-like body-on-frame underpinnings, crossover SUVs including the Honda CR-V use car-like unibody construction. The result is a vehicle that looks like an SUV (and in some instances, performs as well as an SUV—such as the Jeep Grand Cherokee and Land Rover Discovery) and offers the high seating position and—typically—the ground clearance of an SUV, but combines the maneuverability and ride comfort typically associated with cars.

Unlike traditional passenger cars that have a separate trunk around back, hatchbacks combine the passenger compartment and cargo hold into one continuous area. In place of a trunk lid, hatchbacks have a flip-up tailgate, called a "hatch," that can be raised to expose a large storage compartment behind the seats. Hatchbacks typically have either two or four passenger doors plus the hatch, which automakers often classify as an additional door.

The appeal of a rear hatch is rooted in practicality, and that is exactly what traditional hatchbacks are known for. Some models, like the Honda Civic, come in both sedan and hatchback body styles, the latter affording additional cargo volume.

Hot hatchbacks inject some adrenaline into the traditional hatchback formula. Models like the Volkswagen Golf R and Honda Civic Type R are fitted with potent engines and other go-fast features while retaining a rear hatch. That combination makes them equally usable for hefty grocery store runs and weekend track days.

Like sedans, coupes feature a three-box form. Unlike sedans, which feature four doors, coupes come with just two. Coupes tend to prioritize style over practicality, with attractive sloping roofs and limited rear passenger space.

Performance coupes sacrifice nearly everything in the name of high speeds and engaging handling. Two-seat sports cars like the Chevrolet Corvette and Porsche 911 GT3 RS also fall into the performance-coupe category, with mighty engines and sleek body lines being key pillars of the segment.

Luxury coupes take the two-door body style and up the extravagance with opulent cabins and high price tags. The Bentley Continental GT is an exemplar of the luxury-coupe class with quilted leather upholstery and sleek bodywork that oozes style.

In recent years, some automakers have started calling vehicles with sloping rooflines coupes, regardless of their door count or size. The Mercedes CLA-class is an example of a model that is marketed as a four-door coupe. Even some four-door SUVs, such as the BMW iX4, are sold as coupes despite the obvious contradictions.

Convertibles, often called droptops, feature a roof that folds (or drops) away into a compartment behind the passenger compartment for an unfettered view of the sky while cruising. Most convertibles have just two doors, but four-door options do exist. Some convertibles have electrically operated tops that tuck away at the push of a button, while others require the roof to be folded away and raised manually.

Softtop convertibles lack a solid roof and feature a canvas or fabric lid instead. These convertibles tend to weigh less than their hardtop-convertible counterparts.

Instead of using a soft material for the roof, hardtop convertibles feature hard body panels for a roof, which can be folded away—typically at the push of a button, as on the Chevrolet Corvette. Such a setup affords owners the benefits of open-air driving while allowing for additional protection from the elements with the roof in place, including outside noises.

Station wagons are a dying breed. Though they wear a similar shape to many squarebacked SUVs and crossovers, these typically lower-riding machines often share styling fore of the B-pillar (or from the front door forward) with an equivalent sedan in an automaker’s lineup. With no separate trunk and little to no peak in their roofline, station wagons offer a large and versatile cargo hold for hauling items of all sizes.

Luxury station wagons combine the niceties of an automaker's equivalent sedan and pair it with a more cargo-friendly wagon form.

Crossover station wagons, for instance the Audi A6 Allroad, take the basic wagon form and add a bit of (typically pseudo) off-road kit. This normally comes courtesy of unpainted plastic fascias and fender flares, a suspension lift, and standard all-wheel drive. Though these station wagons cannot replace a proper body-on-frame SUV with four-wheel drive off-road, they are capable of handling light off-tarmac terrains.

Pickup trucks are high-riding, utility-focused vehicles that feature a front passenger compartment (known as a "cab") and an open cargo bed in the rear. Most trucks offer some form of all-wheel drive system to improve their off-road and rough-weather capabilities. Pickups range in size from the compact and economical to big and heavy-duty.

Compact pickup trucks trade expansive cargo bed space for efficiency and versatility. While models like the 10Best-winning Ford Maverick and Hyundai Santa Cruz only have enough space in the back for hauling small loads, their small form factor and efficient engines grant them easy maneuverability and relatively impressive fuel economy.

Mid-size pickup trucks strike a balance between size, price, and capability. Mid-sizers such as the Toyota Tacoma and Ford Ranger typically have smaller beds and lower towing capacities than larger full-size and heavy-duty pickups; however, they trade this loss in capability for a smaller footprint and—often—a lower starting price.

Full-size pickup trucks are large and capable trucks with big beds and impressive tow ratings. They are ideal for serious work, but many full-size pickups, including the 10Best-winning Ram 1500 and Ford F-150, are comfortable enough for use as everyday vehicles.

As their name suggests, heavy-duty pickup trucks are meant for heavy hauling. HD workhorses, such as the Ram 2500 and 3500 HD and Ford F-250 and F-350 Super Duty, are easily capable of towing five-figure loads. HD pickups are often available with high-output diesel engines and can be optioned with different cab and bed sizes to suit the needs of multiple rugged professions.

Vans and minivans are known for their spacious insides and box-like exteriors. Both vans and smaller minivans are often long and tall, leaving a cavernous area behind the front seats for either passengers or cargo. Minivans almost unanimously come with one or more sliding rear doors, while bigger vans may include sliding rear doors or a pair of barn doors.

Cargo vans are made for hauling goods. Most come with just two seats, affording plenty of room for carrying cargo aft of the driver and front passenger. In many cases, cargo vans are used as commercial vehicles.

Passenger vans typically take the cargo van template but add a handful of extra exterior windows and multiple rows of rear seats to the mix. Passenger vans often serve as commercial vehicles, though those with a penchant for carrying many passengers will find lots to like in these machines, too.

As their name implies, minivans are, well, smaller-size vans. They're still plenty roomy, though, and typically offer seating for at least seven. With designs that maximize interior space, but a footprint comparable to a three-row mid-size SUV, minivans offer car-like comfort with loads of passenger and cargo room.

#4491. Uber Wants Thousands Of Robotaxis By 2027. Waymo Is Already There

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Uber has racked up a ton of autonomous vehicle partnerships, attempting to position itself as the key platform for driverless rides. And the company has no plans to slow down. On Tuesday, Uber said it wants to spend $10 billion to get 2,000 robotaxis into its global fleet by the end of 2027.

"Our autonomous strategy is entering an important new phase as more of our partners move from development and testing into driverless commercial service," CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in written remarks shared alongside the company's third-quarter earnings.

Around half of those 2,000 robotaxis will be for the United States market, Uber said. The other half will be split up between Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. Uber says the self-driving fleet at that point will span 20 cities and include partnerships with May Mobility, Momenta, Zoox, Motional, and others. By the end of this year, Uber plans to have 700 robotaxis on its platform.

Here's the kicker, though: Even if Uber hits its goal by 2027, it will still be far behind Waymo, which is both a major competitor and, for now, a partner. Waymo, the most prominent robotaxi company in the world, already has a fleet of around 4,000 cars currently on the road, and it currently operates in 15 different U.S. cities.

Waymo aims to double its robotaxi count to 8,000 by the end of the year and hit 20,000 vehicles by the close of 2027, Semafor reported recently. So Uber would still be playing catch-up, big time.

And while users in cities like Atlanta have to use the Uber app to call a Waymo robotaxi, that's changing. Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana told Bloomberg on Wednesday that the company plans to end its exclusivity deal with Uber in Austin and Atlanta in January of 2028. It was “a little bit of a crapshoot,” she said, since Uber customers never knew if they were getting a robotaxi or a human driver.

Uber said its partners have committed to bringing 120,000 robotaxis onto its platform in the coming years, but hasn't put a timeframe on such a lofty goal. It says it's going to fund this fleet of robotaxis with its own earnings, but that it might have to “bring in third-party capital," once its self-driving fleet expands beyond 10,000 cars. Uber claims its gross bookings were up 20%, year-over-year, to the tune of $59.8 billion, so it's got a big book of business to fund its future projects. But with it splitting from Waymo, it's never been more important for the company to get its other partnership projects off the ground and expand them quickly.

#4490. Toyota updates the 2027 RAV4 PHEV with an NACS port and up to 52 miles of EV range

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 is bringing a few major updates, including an added NACS charge port on all plug-in hybrid (PHEV) models.

The RAV4 was Toyota’s best-selling nameplate in the US last year and consistently ranks among America’s most popular vehicles alongside the Ford F-Series and Chevrolet Silverado.

For the 2027 model year, Toyota added several notable upgrades. The 2027 Toyota RAV4 will be available with hybrid (HEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with available front- or all-wheel drive (AWD).

The biggest change is that all 2027 RAV4 PHEV models now have a built-in NACS charge port with Level 3 DC fast-charging capabilities.

The NACS port is on the driver’s side and lets drivers use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. All PHEV grades also include an 11 kW onboard AC charger.

Powered by Toyota’s sixth-generation PHEV system, the plug-in RAV4 has standard AWD with a combined output of 321 horsepower. The setup includes a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, two electric motors, and a high-capacity traction battery.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 PHEV offers up to 52 miles of pure electric range on the base SE trim. It will be available in four trims: SE, XSE, Woodland, and GR Sport.

Toyota updated the suspension system in the Woodland grade for the 2027 model year with new springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers, giving it 9.1″ of ground clearance.

The Woodland trim adds a rugged look with standard All-Terrain tires, Roof Rails with Cross Bars, and a Tow Hitch Receiver. It also features new all-weather floor and cargo mats.

Lastly, the RAV4 GR Sport trim is for those who want a more performance-oriented, sporty style, with GT-tuned suspension and steering, sports seating, and a standard PHEV powertrain with AWD.

Inside, the 2027 RAV4 includes a standard 12.3″ digital cluster and a 10.5″ touchscreen with the Toyota Audio Multimedia system, plus wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

A 12.9″ touchscreen with a JBL Premium Audio system with 9 speakers is standard on the Limited trim and available on the XSE grade.

All 2027 Toyota RAV4s come with standard Toyota Safety Sense 4.0, which includes safety and convenience features such as Lane Departure Alert with Steering Assist, Full-Speed Range Dynamic Radar Cruise Control, Proactive Driving Assist, and a Pre-Collision System with Pedestrian Detection.

They don't make it easy to find out just what that level 3 charging rate is or how big the battery is. If it's as slow as an old Bolt, could take as long as 20 minutes to charge. If the DC charge hardware is more modern, could be 5-10. Would still be a weird choice, but if you need to stop for a drink of a bathroom anyway, why not?

2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV models are expected to begin arriving at dealerships later this year, while the PHEV models are expected to follow in early 2027.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV starts at $32,300 (LE FWD), and the PHEV version starts at $42,100, not including the $1,595 destination fee.

#4489. Ford Says Even the Fathom EV’s Fanciest Trims Will Stay Under $40K

Ford says its top-spec Fathom EV truck will still start well below the average cost of a new car.

Skeptics of the Ford Fathom EV pickup have questioned Ford’s ability to provide a sub-$30,000 truck since its introduction last year, but Andrew Frick, president of Ford’s Model e division, told the Detroit Free Press that even the top trim will remain below $40,000.

After taking a prototype Fathom for a test drive last month, Ford CEO Jim Farley was reportedly blown away by the small truck’s handling and performance, calling it a “breakthrough product.” He also said the Fathom is on track to hit the market toward the end of 2027, though the team will need to keep developing at a rapid pace to get it out on time and within budget.

See all results for new 2028 Ford Fathom for sale near 60629

Ford announced the Fathom’s starting price in August. At $29,945, the pickup truck offers an affordable way to enter the EV world, and it’s the first to ride on Ford’s Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform. The Fathom is already confirmed to be equipped with a touchscreen, built-in Apple Maps, Apple CarPlay, Android Auto, and Blue Cruise hands-free driving capabilities.

The UEV platform operates on a 400-volt electrical architecture, so charging won’t be as quick as vehicles that use an 800-volt system, but Ford says the trade-off for a lighter, more affordable vehicle is worth it. It’ll also use a 48-volt system instead of the traditional 12-volt system used in most vehicles; the higher voltage is intended to increase power and fuel efficiency. Farley revealed this week that the platform will break up the electrical components into five distinct zones to simplify production processes and reduce costs.

The Fathom’s starting price puts it on the more affordable end of the entire car market, including gas-powered and hybrid vehicles, but higher trim levels often bring a significantly higher price to a new car. It’s unclear what will be included in the base model versus the higher specs, but top trims will likely have a longer range, among other upgrades.

The Fathom’s pre-order list is expected to open in the first quarter of 2027, and the truck is slated to go on sale in the last quarter of the year. Pricing beyond the Fathom’s entry point hasn’t yet been announced, but it seems even the highest trim will remain relatively affordable.

#4488. New Jersey is putting 10 MW of community solar on warehouse roofs

Warehouse roofs are prime real estate for solar, and Faropoint is putting more of that underused space to work in New Jersey. The industrial property owner has started construction on the first of 16 community solar projects totaling more than 10 megawatts (MW).

First up is a 1.6 MW rooftop array at 19-05 Nevins Road in Fair Lawn. Another 15 projects, totaling about 8.5 MW, have been accepted into New Jersey’s Community Solar Energy Program, and nine are already cleared to start construction.

That’s more solar going onto buildings that are already there, with participating households set to get savings on their electricity bills.

Large warehouse roofs offer something solar developers need: lots of flat space. Putting panels up there gives the same building the job of generating electricity without taking up additional land.

Faropoint specializes in industrial properties used for local deliveries and distribution. “Utilizing previously unused portions of our buildings allows us to support the communities where we invest,” said Brian Nave, Faropoint’s vice president of asset management and renewable energy.

Faropoint and its independent solar adviser, SolarKal, expect the 16 projects to generate around 12.7 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually once they’re operating. They estimate the portfolio will avoid about 8,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

Faropoint says at least half of each project’s capacity will be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. New Jersey’s program requires a minimum of 51%.

#4487. Waymo And Uber's Robotaxi Partnership Is Ending

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

If you want to ride in a driverless Waymo in Austin or Atlanta, you can currently only do that via the Uber app thanks to an exclusive partnership between the two companies. That will change in 2028 because Waymo has decided to go solo in those two cities.

Waymo Co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana told Bloomberg on Wednesday that the company will exit its partnership with Uber in Austin and Atlanta starting in January 2028. The reason? Mawakana said the Uber app doesn’t guarantee a driverless ride. You can enable autonomous rides via settings in the Uber app, but the chances of one showing up depend on how many Waymos are actually nearby. If there's no Waymo nearby, riders are matched with human drivers.

Uber says it offered to add a dedicated robotaxi ride option through its service so that customers would match with driverless cars more easily, but Waymo reportedly declined that.

“In the early days, we would partner because we didn’t have the scale,” Mawakana told the outlet. "...in that partnering, it was a little bit of a crapshoot," she added.

Customers were now demanding a more consistent experience, Mawakana said. That’s why, starting in January 2028, Waymos in Austin and Atlanta will operate the same way they’ve been operating in over two dozen other U.S. cities: via Waymo’s own dedicated app. With that, current partner Uber will also become a direct rival in those two cities.

The whole point of this partnership was to help Waymo scale and give riders exposure to its cutting-edge driverless technology. Uber is the go-to ride-hail app for millions of riders already. The company also has vast experience in fleet operations and logistics.

Waymo, by comparison, is far smaller but is growing quickly. It’s a fully-owned subsidiary of Google parent Alphabet, which is valued at over $3.5 trillion as of writing. Waymo currently conducts over 500,000 paid driverless trips each week. It’s already operational in 15 U.S. cities and plans to add over a dozen more in the coming months. It's in a comfortable lead in the robotaxi race in the U.S., far ahead of Tesla and others.

It now seems more confident about going solo in Austin and Atlanta. However, it’s still partnering with Lyft for driverless rides in Nashville, although that partnership isn’t exclusive. Waymo also serves Nashville through its own app.

Uber also has grand ambitions when it comes to robotaxis. The company plans to have 700 robotaxis online by the end of this year and 2,000 by the end of 2027. It has emerged as a broker of robotaxi technology, inking deals with several companies including Rivian, Lucid, Wayve, and others to offer their driverless vehicles on the Uber app.

#4486. Segway launches new electric motorcycle that’s so safe it has seatbelts

Segway came to EICMA this year with a surprisingly broad lineup of new electric motorcycles, ranging from high-performance concepts to off-road machines. But perhaps the most interesting of the bunch is also the one that looks the least like a conventional motorcycle or scooter.

Meet the Segway X Cruiser, an electric two-wheeler that takes motorcycle safety so seriously that it has a roll cage and seatbelts.

Or at least, those are among the configurations Segway is showing as it develops the new machine for production.

The X Cruiser is Segway’s attempt to bring more automotive-style protection to a single-track vehicle, essentially asking how much of a car’s safety envelope can be wrapped around a motorcycle without adding another pair of wheels.

From the looks of things, the answer is quite a lot.

Segway says the X Cruiser’s design was informed by automotive crash scenarios, with cage and semi-cage structures, four-direction collision protection, staged energy absorption, and seatbelt restraints intended to improve rider protection. It also gets active safety features including standard blind spot detection and lane change warning.

The company showed several ways that basic idea can be configured, ranging from a more conventional partially enclosed scooter-like setup to versions with significantly more structure surrounding the rider. One of the most striking configurations uses a heavily bolstered race-car-style seat and seatbelt along with protective framing around the rider, while another adds a roof for even more enclosure.

It’s a fascinating approach because motorcycles have traditionally relied largely on the rider wearing the protection. Helmets, jackets, gloves, boots and sometimes airbag vests form the safety system, while the motorcycle itself generally offers little physical protection during a crash.

The X Cruiser effectively flips part of that equation by building some of the protective structure into the vehicle itself.

There’s an important caveat here, though. Segway specifically notes that its descriptions refer to the vehicle’s current design and equipment and do not mean it has completed automotive-style crash certification. Final equipment and certification will depend on individual markets, so it sounds like the company is holding short of making any major certification claims. Still though, it’s easy to see how having what is effectively a racing seat and roll cage surrounding the rider could seriously contribute to better protection in a crash. Just remember to keep your hands and feet within the vehicle at all times.

And unlike plenty of wild EICMA showpieces, this one isn’t merely destined to live under convention-center spotlights. Segway says the X Cruiser has a confirmed mass-production plan, with launches planned for China and Europe between 2027 and 2028. There’s no US availability announcement yet.

Underneath all that protective hardware is a fairly serious electric touring platform. Segway is using its CTB (cell-to-body) battery integration to help improve structural rigidity and battery packaging, with the company targeting nearly 200 km (124 miles) of range.

European versions are expected to feature 4.5 kW Type 2 AC charging, while the Chinese version will offer optional higher-power DC fast charging. The bike rolls on 15-inch front and 14-inch rear wheels wearing Michelin City Grip tires, and riders get a 10.25-inch TFT display along with an optional 55-liter electrically operated top box.

Interestingly, the X Cruiser also incorporates certain two-wheeler intellectual property and know-how licensed from BMW Group, though Segway stresses that it is responsible for the vehicle’s development, integration, validation, production and certification.

The X Cruiser may be the weirdest – and thus perhaps the most interesting – of Segway’s EICMA debuts, but it was far from alone.

The company also unveiled the Segway Orca Concept, a futuristic high-performance electric maxi-scooter concept built around an 800V electrical architecture and a nearly 20 kWh battery.

Segway is targeting up to 300 km (186 miles) of range, a 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) time of 4.5 seconds, and the ability to add 200 km (124 miles) of range in 20 minutes. The concept also features front and rear multi-link suspension, electronically controlled multi-mode damping and a battery-integrated CTB chassis. Those figures are engineering targets rather than promised production specifications, and Segway currently describes the Orca strictly as a concept.

Its a BMW C1 reborn as electric! They were a bit of a cult thing, but underpowered for the weight. Never made it to the USA.

The biggest benefit is not really safety, its comfort.

Then there’s Segway’s expanding X Series, which moves the focus away from urban riding and toward dirt. The lineup includes the Xaber X1000 and Xaber 350, along with different Xaber 300 variants for the US and European markets. Segway is also partnering with Michelin for its Dakar Rally Factory Team, using the brutal rally environment as a real-world development and validation platform for electric off-road motorcycles.

Taken together, it’s quite the showing from a company whose name many people still associate primarily with those funny two-wheeled self-balancing machines from the early 2000s.

Segway has already expanded heavily into electric scooters, e-bikes, go-karts and powersports vehicles. Now it seems increasingly serious about becoming an electric motorcycle company as well.

And if motorcycles with roll cages, roofs and seatbelts are part of that future, things could get pretty interesting… pretty quickly!

#4484. Tesla Sold FSD To Koreans Who Still Can't Use It. Now It's Facing A Complaint

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Tesla's Full Self-Driving will turn 10 years old next month. Nearly four of those years have labeled FSD as an official beta product, and over two additional years have been under the new "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)" rebranding. Whatever the name, the car that is in your driveway today still can't technically drive itself without you being responsible for what happens behind the wheel.

Needless to say, some drivers are getting impatient—especially those who have purchased FSD for multiple cars, or have managed to pay off their car loan before getting unsupervised FSD. Now a consumer advocacy group in South Korea is firing back to demand answers and accountability.

The rollout of FSD in Korea is even more confusing that it is in the U.S. thanks to another layer of complexity: where the vehicle was manufactured.

According to Reuters, only about 20% of the Teslas registered in South Korea—vehicles assembled in the United States—are actually eligible to enable the Full Self-Driving software. That's because those vehicles meet the U.S. Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards, and a trade agreement with the U.S. designates those standards as acceptable to enter Korea without additional modification.

The majority of the remaining vehicles have been manufactured in China, where no agreement (or supplementary safety certification) for its FSD software exists today. Since 2023, Tesla has imported about 170,000 of these Shanghai-built cars with the volume of Chinese-built cars increasing five-fold last year alone. In fact, 99% of Teslas imported into China in 2025 were from China and ineligible to activate FSD.

A complaint being filed by Korean consumer advocacy group Citizens United for Consumer Sovereignty (reviewed by Reuters) with the Korean Fair Trade Commission alleges that Tesla has still been collecting money from buyers for its FSD software for over three years, despite the software not being available to buyers due to this restriction. This meant buyers forked over as much as $6,800 for the feature, but haven't actually been able to switch it on. Some buyers instead resorted to enabling region-locked FSD via a "jailbreak," which is seen as a safety circumvention and led to owners facing jail time or fines of up to $15,000.

Things get a bit more complicated given the recent legal loss raised by dozens of Tesla owners who had their lawsuit thrown out of Korean courts just last week. According to the ruling from the Seoul Central District Court, Tesla didn't technically break its contractual obligations with the 88 owners who requested full refunds via a lawsuit filed in 2024.

The court acknowledged that Tesla's delivery of the features promised with FSD hinged on certain technical advances and regulatory approval that buyers were aware could "take considerable time to become available," according to reporting by the South China Morning Post. If those didn't happen, the court says that Tesla isn't in the wrong.

The complaint by Citizens United raises additional questions about the way that Tesla advertises its vehicles to consumers. And they're not the first. The KFTC confirmed to Reuters that it launched a probe into Tesla's advertising earlier this year, but declined to comment further. Tesla didn't respond to the outlet's request for comment.

Whether or not this avenue will result in action after the court's ruling that buyers weren't entitled to a refund is unclear.

#4483. 10 Pokémon That Are the Biggest Green Flags

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

There have been many Pokémon over the years. When you combine all the generations, there are over 1,000 different Pokémon, and each one is bound to be somebody’s favorite.

Of course, not every Pokémon conveys a positive message. There are some Pokémon, who, when mentioned as someone’s favorite, give off some major red flags.

On the other hand, there are Pokémon that also give off some major green flags. These are Pokémon that show you can trust a person. Maybe they are motherly, maybe they are a great friend, or maybe they are as innocent as can be. Either way, they are great to have around.

Mew is a classic Pokémon that is usually loved by everyone in the fan base, with few people considering it a negative sign. The reason for this is that Mew is just a little guy who is generally sweet towards others.

If you take one look at Mew, you can easily tell that it is a green flag. It looks absolutely harmless, and wouldn’t hurt a fly unless it was specifically required to do so.

With Mew being so harmless, anyone who chooses this Pokémon as their favorite is considered to be a sweet and empathetic individual who just wants to be around others because it makes them happy.

Mimikyu somewhat tows the line between a red flag and a green flag, but I am here to tell you that this Pokémon is for sure a green flag. The argument about it being a red flag is mostly because it is trying too hard to be Pikachu.

However, if you choose Mimikyu as your favorite Pokémon, it is probably because you have the emotional intelligence to identify with Mimikyu and recognize that it just wants to be loved.

It is a misunderstood creature who dresses up as Pikachu to hopefully one day get the love it rightfully deserves, which makes those who love this Pokémon people who recognize it for what it is, and realize that it is a lonesome creature who just wants to be seen.

Some Pokedex entries in the Pokemon series are pretty brutal, and these are the saddest.

The legendary beast trio from generation two are some of the most recognizable legendary Pokémon from the franchise. While each of these Pokémon are a green flag, I chose Entei to represent them because I feel like it is the most well-liked.

The legendary beasts are a great pull from the second generation of Pokémon that are well-known enough that it isn’t weird, and they aren’t obscure enough that it feels like you are trying too hard.

Each of the legendary beasts are known for being protectors, but Entei has the greatest appearance of them, coming off as more of a large fluffy lion, giving it more of the guardian vibes that people who love this Pokémon may themselves embody.

Wooloo is a more recent pull from generation eight, as the Pokémon made its first appearance in Pokémon Sword and Shield. Those who have played these games know that Wooloo are found in plenty of places early in the game, with its white wool covering the fields of Paldea.

Wooloo is an innocent little buddy who is calm, doesn’t want to go into a fight, and would rather just chill. Its little pigtails that hang along the sides of its face make it even more approachable.

Those who love this Pokémon are perceived as loving, calm, and big softies who wouldn’t want to fight unless it's absolutely necessary. The only one that is a red flag is Hop’s Wooloo, and that’s only because it beat me in the game that one time.

Every pocket monster in Pokopia is beautiful in its own way, but some are cuter than others.

Teddiursa has been around for a long time. In fact, it has been in the games since generation two, meaning fans have had a long time with this Pokémon, and there are some who consider it their favorite.

You’ll notice that many of the Pokémon on this list match the theme of “little guys,” and that is because they are so sweet and innocent that you don’t need to worry about them. Teddiursa is one of them, where it just wants to play around and eat some honey.

Those who love Teddiursa have a cute and playful side. They are also generally viewed as non-toxic because they would rather just have fun and cozy up by the fire with a good book.

There is a theme of Pokémon who are considered the “derpy” ones, and Fuecoco falls very specifically into that category. It has a face that screams, “I just want to sit around and snack all day without worrying about stressful things.”

Fuecoco is the definition of someone who is ignorant to the world around them and is blissfully going about life at their own pace. They have little care in the world and that is perfectly fine because it makes them happy.

There’s little that could be considered wrong with someone who likes Fuecoco. Maybe they are a bit too childish at times, but they are overall just a good person who lives the way they want.

Lapras is one of Ash’s Pokémon from the anime, and a Pokémon that stands out from the first generation. It is cute, calm, and collected, meaning it is definitely a green flag Pokémon.

If you judge the Pokémon from its Pokédex entry, you will find that it has a gentle heart, which led to many of them being caught because they rarely fight. Plus, it loves to ferry people around on its back, showing that you pride yourself on being there for others.

Additionally, Lapras is an overall intelligent Pokémon that is capable of understanding human speech, and those who choose it as their favorite Pokémon are often showing that they are caring, intelligent, and emotionally available friends who just want to be there for their pals.

There are some Pokémon where it feels like you chose it to be cool or to follow a trend. Cough. Charizard. Cough. Then there are some Pokémon where you love them despite the popularity, accepting the fact that they aren’t the best in terms of stats, but rather, they are just cute.

Eevee is one of those cute Pokémon that is beloved by everyone, and some choose Eevee as their favorite because of how adorable it is. Also, an argument can be made about its potential, with those who love this Pokémon showing that they believe they have great potential in life in the same way Eevee does through its evolutions.

This is a safe, friendly, and easy pick for many. It may be a bit too basic for some, but the cute factor solidifies it as a top-tier green flag.

Psyduck is a great choice for a favorite Pokémon, and is a major green flag. I am totally not saying that because it is one of my favorites, but rather because it is relatable.

This Pokémon suffers from constant headaches, which many can relate to because of the stresses of life constantly feeling like they're weighing them down. Psyduck feels like the embodiment of what is in people’s minds when dealing with stress, and it feels like an outlet in a sense.

Plus, Psyduck has some of the cutest expressions, with it often conveying confusions, annoyance, and more. If you love Psyduck, you probably aren’t toxic, have a decent sense of humor, and can be a bit childish. Now, I will pat myself on the back.

The biggest green flag of the entire Pokédex belongs to two Pokémon, and they are Wooper and Quagsire. Since I can only choose one, I went with Quagsire. After all, it is just a bigger version of Wooper.

We need to give those who love Quagsire a big hug and thank them for being some of the most chill and down to Earth people out there, as this choice of favorite is one that shows that they have the ability to just go with the flow, accepting life as it is.

Quagsire is the definition of a Pokémon that just doesn’t care about the stresses of life and lets them slide off its body and into the water it floats around in. Thanks for being such a special soul Quagsire, and keep up that chill lifestyle.

From the Eevee evolutions to Magikarp becoming something useful, here are the Pokémon in FireRed and LeafGreen that feel different after evolving.

#4482. BYD’s newest EV is about as big as a Toyota Camry, but brings a lot more tech for $23K

BYD launched the new Seal 07 in China, where it starts at around $23,000. It’s about the size of a Toyota Camry, but brings a surprising amount of tech and premium features for the money.

After introducing the updated first-generation Seal 07 in March, BYD launched the second-gen model on Thursday.

The second-generation Seal 07, which BYD calls the “new choice for a class-leading luxury experience,” is available in battery electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains.

BYD offers five variants, including two PHEVs and three EVs, starting at 139,900 yuan (about $21,000) for the plug-in hybrid and 149,900 yuan (around $22,500) for the fully electric version.

The new Seal 07 EV uses a 76.7 kWh second-generation BYD Blade LFP battery, providing a CLTC range of up to 481 miles (775 km).

It comes standard with a single rear-mounted electric motor producing up to 328 hp (245 kW) and 269 lb-ft (365 Nm) of torque, which BYD says enables it to accelerate from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 5.5 seconds.

All plug-in hybrid variants use BYD’s latest DM-i system, which features a 1.5L turbocharged engine with 154 hp (115 kW) and a 214 hp (160 kW) front electric motor.

The new Seal 07 PHEV has a smaller 37 kWh battery that provides up to 205 miles (330 km) of pure electric CLTC range. That’s a considerable jump from the 143 miles (230 km) of electric range the previous generation offered.

Thanks to BYD’s latest Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, the vehicle’s battery can recharge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes. To go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

Both versions are 5,080 mm long, 1,960 mm wide, and 1,495 mm tall, with a 2,960 mm wheelbase, which is slightly bigger than the Toyota Camry.

Inside, the new Seal 07 adopts BYD’s latest cabin design, including a 15.6″ floating center infotainment screen, a 10.25″ instrument cluster, and two rear passenger entertainment screens.

BYD added several premium extras, including a built-in 6.8L smart refrigerator, zero gravity seats, and driver headrest audio. It also offers the most rear passenger space and the largest frunk (160L) in its class, according to BYD.

The Seal 07 debuts BYD’s Smart Ecosystem 2.0, including “Diva,” a smartwatch that can interact with the vehicle and let drivers manage functions remotely.

Higher-priced models offer BYD’s God’s Eye B intelligent driving system, with a roof-mounted LiDAR available as an option. The setup provides safety and convenience features such as Navigation on Autopilot in the city and on highways, plus full-scenario intelligent parking.

BYD is offering a limited-time “Super trade-in price” promo, starting at 145,900 yuan ($22,000) for the new Seal 07 EV and 135,900 yuan ($20,500) for the PHEV version.
